The new candidate for empire saw and improved the peculiar       advantage of his situation. His province extended to the Julian       Alps, which gave an easy access into Italy; and he remembered the       saying of Augustus, that a Pannonian army might in ten days       appear in sight of Rome. 31 By a celerity proportioned to the       greatness of the occasion, he might reasonably hope to revenge       Pertinax, punish Julian, and receive the homage of the senate and       people, as their lawful emperor, before his competitors,       separated from Italy by an immense tract of sea and land, were       apprised of his success, or even of his election. During the       whole expedition, he scarcely allowed himself any moments for       sleep or food; marching on foot, and in complete armor, at the       head of his columns, he insinuated himself into the confidence       and affection of his troops, pressed their diligence, revived       their spirits, animated their hopes, and was well satisfied to       share the hardships of the meanest soldier, whilst he kept in       view the infinite superiority of his reward.

The wretched Julian had expected, and thought himself prepared,       to dispute the empire with the governor of Syria; but in the       invincible and rapid approach of the Pannonian legions, he saw       his inevitable ruin. The hasty arrival of every messenger       increased his just apprehensions. He was successively informed,       that Severus had passed the Alps; that the Italian cities,       unwilling or unable to oppose his progress, had received him with       the warmest professions of joy and duty; that the important place       of Ravenna had surrendered without resistance, and that the       Hadriatic fleet was in the hands of the conqueror. The enemy was       now within two hundred and fifty miles of Rome; and every moment       diminished the narrow span of life and empire allotted to Julian.

He attempted, however, to prevent, or at least to protract, his       ruin. He implored the venal faith of the Prætorians, filled the       city with unavailing preparations for war, drew lines round the       suburbs, and even strengthened the fortifications of the palace;       as if those last intrenchments could be defended, without hope of       relief, against a victorious invader. Fear and shame prevented       the guards from deserting his standard; but they trembled at the       name of the Pannonian legions, commanded by an experienced       general, and accustomed to vanquish the barbarians on the frozen       Danube. 32 They quitted, with a sigh, the pleasures of the baths       and theatres, to put on arms, whose use they had almost       forgotten, and beneath the weight of which they were oppressed.       The unpractised elephants, whose uncouth appearance, it was       hoped, would strike terror into the army of the north, threw       their unskilful riders; and the awkward evolutions of the       marines, drawn from the fleet of Misenum, were an object of       ridicule to the populace; whilst the senate enjoyed, with secret       pleasure, the distress and weakness of the usurper. 33

**Main argument**

The passage is a sustained argument that the accession of Septimius Severus was made possible – and in fact inevitable – by the geographic and military advantage of his position in Pannonia.  By stressing the ease with which a Pannonian army could cross the Julian Alps and reach Italy, the author shows that Severus could have proclaimed himself emperor and, within a few weeks, marched on Rome before any of his rivals (especially Julian) had a realistic chance to react.  In other words, the text tries to prove that the “original contract”‑type explanation of imperial legitimacy (as advanced by scholars such as Hume) is inadequate: Severus’ claim rested on speed, location and the loyalty of his troops, not merely on a formal agreement with the army.

**Evidence supporting the claim**

1. **Geographic advantage** – The author points out that Severus’ province “extended to the Julian Alps, which gave an easy access into Italy.”  This physical description (the proximity of the Danube frontier to the Po plain) is the foundation of the argument; the shorter the distance, the quicker the march.

2. **Augustus’ proverb** – The quotation that “a Pannonian army might in ten days appear in sight of Rome” (cited from Augustus) is invoked as a historic precedent for the rapid mobility of Pannonian troops.  Its inclusion frames Severus’ movement as a continuation of Roman strategic tradition.

3. **Velleius Paterculus’ marching estimate** – The footnote records that Velleius calculates the march from the “nearest verge of Pannonia” to sight of Rome as covering two hundred miles.  This quantitative detail underscores the feasibility of a ten‑day crossing and lends a sense of precision to the claim that Severus could have reached Italy swiftly.

4. **Contemporary reports of Italian submission** – The narrative relates that “the Italian cities, unwilling or unable to oppose his progress, had received him with the warmest professions of joy and duty.”  Such accounts (drawn from Herodian, Victor, etc.) demonstrate that once Severus entered Italy he was already encountering a de‑facto acceptance, reinforcing the idea that his advance rendered any opposition superfluous.

5. **Strategic successes in the north** – The text notes that “Ravenna had surrendered without resistance, and that the Hadriatic fleet was in the hands of the conqueror.”  The loss of these key naval and logistical bases further illustrates how quickly Severus could neutralise the defensive resources of the empire.

6. **Julian’s panic and impotence** – Julian’s reaction is presented as one of “trembling perplexity.”  He receives successive messengers reporting Severus’ crossing of the Alps, the Italian welcome, and the loss of Ravenna.  The author highlights Julian’s frantic attempts to fortify the palace, to win the Praetorian support, and even to employ magic – all of which are portrayed as desperate and ultimately futile.  Julian’s inability to muster an effective response supplies further proof that Severus’ geographic advantage placed him in a position of irreversible strength.

7. **Contradictions over the proclamation site** – The footnote on Carnuntum versus Sabaria (Spartianus vs. Victor) shows that while the exact spot of Severus’ proclamation is uncertain, both locations lie on the Danube frontier.  The author’s point is that whichever site he chose, he still possessed the same strategic proximity to Italy; thus the argument is not dependent on a precise location but on the broader advantage of the Pannonian region.

8. **Critique of Hume’s “original contract” theory** – By citing Hume’s essay and noting that he “has not considered this transaction with his usual accuracy,” the author signals that the real factor in Severus’ rise is the swift military reality described above, not a formal contractual arrangement.  This meta‑historical comment frames the narrative as a corrective to a scholarly debate.

**Synthesis**

Taken together, these pieces of evidence construct a coherent case: Severus’ claim to the imperial throne was underpinned by a concrete, exploitable geographic advantage.  The distance from Pannonia to Italy, the precedent of Augustus’ proverb, the quantitative march reported by Velleius, and the rapid capitulation of key Italian and northern strongholds all combine to show that he could, and did, secure imperial legitimacy far more through speed and military might than through any abstract “contract” with the army.  Consequently, the author argues that the instability of the Year of the Four Emperors was in part a function of how quickly a capable general, backed by his troops and a favorable frontier, could translate his position into imperial power.

- **Consequences:**  This autocratic turn **undermines the Senate’s real authority**, makes the republican theory “insensible” and gives way to the “natural and substantial feelings of monarchy.”  The loss of republican legitimacy, combined with the growing power of the military and the legal doctrine that the Senate “irrevocably resigned” its powers, sets the stage for the **gradual decline of the Roman Empire**.  
- **Illustrative evidence:**  
  - The Senate, now filled with “polished and eloquent slaves” from the East, becomes a **figment** that merely justifies passive obedience.  
  - Roman jurists (Papinian, Paulus, Ulpian) codify the idea that the emperor’s will is law, treating the empire as his **private patrimony**.

This latent civil war already distracted the whole government,       when a scheme was suggested that seemed of mutual benefit to the       hostile brothers. It was proposed, that since it was impossible       to reconcile their minds, they should separate their interest,       and divide the empire between them. The conditions of the treaty       were already drawn with some accuracy. It was agreed that       Caracalla, as the elder brother should remain in possession of       Europe and the western Africa; and that he should relinquish the       sovereignty of Asia and Egypt to Geta, who might fix his       residence at Alexandria or Antioch, cities little inferior to       Rome itself in wealth and greatness; that numerous armies should       be constantly encamped on either side of the Thracian Bosphorus,       to guard the frontiers of the rival monarchies; and that the       senators of European extraction should acknowledge the sovereign       of Rome, whilst the natives of Asia followed the emperor of the       East. The tears of the empress Julia interrupted the negotiation,       the first idea of which had filled every Roman breast with       surprise and indignation. The mighty mass of conquest was so       intimately united by the hand of time and policy, that it       required the most forcible violence to rend it asunder. The       Romans had reason to dread, that the disjointed members would       soon be reduced by a civil war under the dominion of one master;       but if the separation was permanent, the division of the       provinces must terminate in the dissolution of an empire whose       unity had hitherto remained inviolate. 20

Had the treaty been carried into execution, the sovereign of       Europe might soon have been the conqueror of Asia; but Caracalla       obtained an easier, though a more guilty, victory. He artfully       listened to his mother’s entreaties, and consented to meet his       brother in her apartment, on terms of peace and reconciliation.       In the midst of their conversation, some centurions, who had       contrived to conceal themselves, rushed with drawn swords upon       the unfortunate Geta. His distracted mother strove to protect him       in her arms; but, in the unavailing struggle, she was wounded in       the hand, and covered with the blood of her younger son, while       she saw the elder animating and assisting 21 the fury of the       assassins. As soon as the deed was perpetrated, Caracalla, with       hasty steps, and horror in his countenance, ran towards the       Prætorian camp, as his only refuge, and threw himself on the       ground before the statues of the tutelar deities. 22 The soldiers       attempted to raise and comfort him. In broken and disordered       words he informed them of his imminent danger, and fortunate       escape; insinuating that he had prevented the designs of his       enemy, and declared his resolution to live and die with his       faithful troops. Geta had been the favorite of the soldiers; but       complaint was useless, revenge was dangerous, and they still       reverenced the son of Severus. Their discontent died away in idle       murmurs, and Caracalla soon convinced them of the justice of his       cause, by distributing in one lavish donative the accumulated       treasures of his father’s reign. 23 The real _sentiments_ of the       soldiers alone were of importance to his power or safety. Their       declaration in his favor commanded the dutiful _professions_ of       the senate. The obsequious assembly was always prepared to ratify       the decision of fortune; 231 but as Caracalla wished to assuage       the first emotions of public indignation, the name of Geta was       mentioned with decency, and he received the funeral honors of a       Roman emperor. 24 Posterity, in pity to his misfortune, has cast       a veil over his vices. ### 1. Main Argument

The passage sets out a clear moral indictment of Emperor Caracalla.  It argues that Caracalla’s murder of his brother Geta, his subsequent proscriptions, and his cynical manipulation of “necessity” and “virtue” expose a tyrant who is both a hypocritical ruler and a murderous conspirator. The passage is a moral‑political indictment of **Macrinus**.  By pointing out that his indecision, cowardice and “shameful flight” allowed a “young pretender” (the Antoninus who claimed to be the rightful heir of Severus) to rally the Syrian armies, the author argues that Macrinus’s weakness was the decisive factor in his downfall.  The narrative does two things at once:

* **Chronological legitimation** – the opening paragraph (Lampridius vs. Herodian) is used to show that the “young princes” (Alexander Severus and his cousin‑emperor Elagabalus) were older than Herodian’s account allows, thereby underscoring the fact that the empire was being ruled by adolescent emperors who were ill‑equipped for war.  This chronological correction is the author’s way of explaining why Macrinus, a similarly youthful ruler, could not command the loyalty of the army.

* **Moral exemplar** – the “conspiracy of women and eunuchs” and the “spirit of rebellion” that spreads through the Syrian camps are presented as a rational, even prudent, reaction to Macrinus’s “tardy restitution of pay and privileges.”  The rebels, especially the eunuch **Gannys**, are praised as “able and experienced generals,” while the troops’ “drooping courage” is sparked into action by the mothers and grand‑mothers who throw themselves from their chariots.  In contrast, Macrinus “floated between the opposite extremes of terror and security,” is “inactive at Antioch,” and when the battle turns his way he “betrays his own cause by a shameful and precipitate flight.”  The passage therefore argues that true Roman virtue lies in steadfast leadership and the willingness to fight for one’s emperor; Macrinus’s failure in these respects makes him a fit object of condemnation.

In short, the text’s central claim is that **Macrinus’s youthful indecision and cowardice, exposed by the prudent conspiracy of his enemies, inevitably led to his defeat and to the rise of the more capable (though still youthful) pretender Antoninus**.  The chronological note serves only to reinforce the idea that the empire was being ruled by adolescent emperors who lacked the experience to command the army.

The passage is a compact, “Whig‑style” diagnosis of the empire’s deterioration in the late‑third century.  Gibbon (the “G” at the end of the foot‑note) is not simply recounting events; he is arguing that the *personal failings of the emperors* and the *ever‑growing power of the army* were the decisive forces that turned a once‑vigorous state into a “faint image of laws and liberty”.  Alexander Severus is held up as the textbook example of this thesis:

* his “amiable” character is shown to be inadequate to the “difficulties of his situation”;  
* his mother’s avarice and the “soft climate of Syria” have corrupted him;  
* his military successes (the Persian campaign) are doubtful, and the contradictory accounts of Herodian, Eusebius, etc., reveal that the triumph was at best a modest, perhaps fabricated, triumph.  

From Alexander’s shortcomings Gibbon moves to the broader pattern: the “dissolute tyranny of Commodus”, the civil wars after his death, and the “new maxims of policy” of the Severan house all “increased the dangerous power of the army” and eroded republican liberty.  Finally, the passage points to Caracalla’s 212 AD citizenship edict as a symptom of the empire’s fiscal and political decay—an “unbounded liberality” that, in Gibbon’s view, stems from “avarice” rather than genuine generosity.  In short, the author’s central claim is that the empire’s decline is not a distant, abstract process but a chain of *human* failures—weak rulers, corrupt families, and a militarised polity—that can be traced directly from the reign of Alexander Severus to the reforms of Caracalla.

### 1.  What the passage is doing  

The passage is not a straightforward “report of events.”  It is a *rhetorical* historiographical sketch that aims to **explain the downfall of Alexander Severus as the inevitable consequence of military disaffection and the opportunistic machinations of the usurper Maximin**.  The author repeatedly frames the episode as a moral lesson about the dangers of an emperor who loses the army’s confidence, and he does so by invoking the authority of earlier imperial historians (the foot‑note references to the *Historia Augusta*, Herodian, etc.).  In other words, the central argument is political‑psychological rather than strictly factual: *the emperor’s legitimacy was eroded by the soldiers’ resentment, and Maximin seized the moment by promising them a “real soldier” who would restore Roman vigor.*  

Take, for example, the opening clause:

Here the narrator does not merely recount that Maximin was a Thracian usurper; he *interprets* the favor‑exchange as a catalyst for the soldier‑class’s ambition, setting up the causal chain that leads to Alexander’s murder. 1. **The “Crisis of the Third Century” (c. 235‑284).**  The period was marked by rapid turnover of emperors, frequent usurpations, and a growing reliance on the army to legitimize rule.  Alexander Severus (r. 222‑233) had attempted reforms that made him appear “effeminate” to traditional Roman sensibilities: he cultivated a scholarly education, softened military discipline, and was married to the Syrian princess **Mamæa**, whose Syrian origin was portrayed as a foreign, decadent influence. ## 1. Main Argument

Firmus argues that the Roman Senate’s decision to ratify the proclamation of the two Gordians as emperors and to brand Maximin and his supporters as enemies of the Republic was both **prudent** and **morally justifiable**.  His case rests on three inter‑related points:

1. **Self‑preservation of the Senate** – The Senate, aware of Maximin’s ruthless tyranny and the danger he posed to their lives and liberty, concluded that only by aligning with the Gordians could they safeguard themselves.  The “care of their own safety” (the “cogitatione propriæ tutæ”) pushes them to act.

2. **Restoration of liberty and humanity** – The Senate frames the Gordians’ elevation as the fulfillment of a long‑standing desire to “return thanks … to the youth of Thysdrus” and “to the faithful people of Carthage,” who have delivered Rome from a “horrid monster.”  By doing so they claim to be reviving not only the imperial office but also the *republican* spirit of freedom.

3. **Moral condemnation of Maximin** – Maximin is portrayed as an implacable enemy whose “hatred” and “fury” cannot be appeased by mere submission.  The Senate’s decree that he and his adherents be “enemies of their country” and that “liberal rewards” be offered to those who destroy him underscores the view that his rule is a tyrannical violation of the common good.

Through these arguments Firmus presents the Senate’s choice as a rational, ethically necessary response to tyranny, thereby legitimising the Gordians’ accession and the subsequent military revolt against Maximin.

---

## 2. Rhetorical Style

| Feature | How it is used in the passage |
|---------|--------------------------------|
| **Elevated diction & classical allusion** | Phrases such as “the noble ardor of the consul,” “the prudence and felicity of Gordian the father,” and “the valor and constancy of Gordian the son” echo the language of Roman historiography and moral philosophy. |
| **Rhetorical questions** | “Why do you hear me thus coolly, thus timidly? Why do you cast those anxious looks on each other? Why hesitate?” – these questions seek to stir the Senate’s emotions and force a decisive response. |
| **Antithesis & parallelism** | The contrast between Maximin’s “public enemy” status and the Gordians’ “restoration of civil and republican government” creates a clear moral polarity; enumerations of the Senate’s motives (“their fortune created many dependants… their merit acquired many friends”) employ parallel structure for emphasis. |
| **Appeal to authority (ethos)** | The footnotes repeatedly cite Victor and the *Historia Augusta*, signalling that the argument is grounded in respected ancient testimony and thus lending it credibility. |
| **Pathos** | Vivid imagery (“the statues of Maximin were thrown down,” “the capital of the empire acknowledged, with transport, the authority of the two Gordians”) evokes the emotional impact of liberty’s restoration on both the Senate and the Roman populace. |
| **Structured argumentation** | The passage moves from a description of the Senate’s deliberations, through the speech of Consul Syllanus, to the decree’s enactment, and finally to the broader political consequences, mirroring the logical progression of classical rhetorical speeches. |

Overall, Firmus adopts the style of a late‑antique Roman historian‑philosopher: sober, didactic, and heavily indebted to classical models of persuasion.

## 3. Historical Context

1. **Year of the Five Emperors (AD 180‑182)** – The passage reflects the chaotic power vacuum that followed Commodus’s assassination.  Various claimants—Maximin, the Gordians, and later Septimius Severus— vied for control.  The Senate, traditionally marginal in this period, attempts to reassert its authority by supporting the African‑based Gordians.

2. **African support for the Gordians** – The African legions, under the command of the Gordian brothers (likely the *Gordiani brothers* who later became co‑emperors in Africa), proclaim them “emperors by the general consent of Africa.”  This underscores the geographical fragmentation of the empire and the Senate’s reliance on provincial loyalty.

3. **Maximin’s tyranny** – Maximin (the younger) is portrayed as a cruel, oppressive ruler whose “hatred” and “fury” threaten the Roman *mos maiorum* (custom of the ancestors). 5. **Historiographical tradition** – By citing Victor and the *Historia Augusta*, Firmus situates his analysis within the late‑antique historiographical canon that treated imperial events as moral exempla. **1. Main Argument**

The passage is a compact historiographical essay whose central claim can be summed up in three inter‑locking points:

1. **The fall of Maximinus Thrax was a turning‑point that promised a return to “civil” rule.**  
   The text opens with the “universal joy of the Roman world” at the tyrant’s death, the triumphal entry of Maximus and Balbinus, and the expectation that a “golden age” would follow the “age of iron.” The emperor’s oppressive taxes, the restoration of justice “in person,” and the revival of discipline are presented as concrete steps toward a healthier polity.

2. **The relationship between the empire and its soldiers is precarious and morally ambiguous.**  
   Balbinus’s apprehension—“alas! I dread the hatred of the soldiers, and the fatal effects of their resentment”—is taken as a warning that the army can become a source of disorder. The narrative of the ensuing civil war, the mutinous Praetorians, and the “infinite loss and confusion” on both sides illustrates how the soldiers’ power can undermine the very state they are supposed to defend.

3. **True stability requires a disciplined, loyal army that submits to senatorial and imperial authority, but the reverse is also possible.**  
   The author repeatedly stresses that the Senate must “administer justice in person” and enact “wise laws” to restore a civil constitution. At the same time, he concedes that “if they had courage to despise the vain terrors of an impotent republic, it was easy to convince the world, that those who were masters of the arms, were masters of the authority, of the state.” In other words, the soldiers are both the empire’s greatest resource and its greatest danger; only proper leadership can prevent them from becoming masters in their own right.

Thus the passage argues that the fall of Maximinus opened a brief window for a return to lawful, civilian‑led government, yet the success of that window depended on keeping the army under strict moral and political control.

2. **Necessary Subordination**  
   The ideal expressed is a hierarchical one: *senatores* and *princeps* must command, not be commanded. The passage urges “the soldiers must now learn a new doctrine of submission to the senate,” and the Senate must “administer justice in person” and “enact wise laws.”

3. **Rewarding Loyalty, Not Dominating It**  
   Maximus’s “liberal donative,” “solemn sacrifice of expiation,” and the promise that “the senate would remember only their generous desertion” illustrate that the historian sees proper reward as the key to securing loyalty.

   By emphasising that “the conduct of the two emperors corresponded with these expectations” and that “many wise laws were enacted by their imperial ministers, who endeavored to restore a civil constitution,” the author places moral onus on the civilian leadership to keep the army in check.

Their policy, though initially effective, proved disastrous for both their own reigns and the empire, for the princes soon fell into petty rivalry, failing to unite against a sudden assault by desperate assassins and the Praetorian guard. The author adopts the tone of a eighteenth‑ or nineteenth‑century classical historian, reminiscent of Edward Gibbon or the French Enlightenment scholars. The prose is formal, heavily annotated with footnote‑like brackets, and peppered with learned citations (“Hist. August. p. 170”, “Quintus Curtius l. x. c. 9”). The diction is elevated (“the senate elected two princes”, “the jealousy of power”, “the silent discord was understood rather than seen”) and the narrative proceeds in a sequential, almost story‑like fashion, punctuated by moral judgments (“their policy was effectual, but it proved fatal”). The rhetorical devices—parallelism (“their silent discord … prevented them from uniting”), irony (“their emperors were left almost alone in the palace”), and frequent use of Latin quotations—serve to reinforce the author’s didactic intent, presenting history as a lesson on the perils of factionalism and the instability of imperial succession.

**Historical context**  
The passage reflects the chaotic phase known as the Crisis of the Third Century (c. 235‑284 CE), when rapid turnover among emperors, military usurpations, and internal strife threatened the Roman state. The scenario of two co‑emperors—Maximus and Balbinus—echoes the actual historical episode of 238 CE, when the joint accession of these brothers (or cousins) was short‑lived, culminating in their assassination. The passage is a composite of secondary scholarship rather than a primary source. ### (a) Retell the story (plot) in your own words  

The passage describes the central doctrine of Zoroastrian theology—the *two‑principle* system. According to the text, the universe is governed by an infinite, timeless principle (referred to in Zoroaster’s writings as “Time without bounds”). From this primal source emerged two eternal, active forces: **Ormuzd** (the principle of good) and **Ahriman** (the principle of evil). Ormuzd is portrayed as benevolent, creating humanity capable of virtue, arranging the heavens, earth, and the elements in harmonious order. Ahriman, however, is malicious; he “pierced Ormuzd’s egg,” breaking the original harmony. After this rupture, good and evil are interwoven in the world: poisonous plants grow among healing ones, natural disasters (floods, earthquakes, fire) testify to the ongoing conflict. Humanity is besieged by vice and misfortune, with most people being led captive by Ahriman. Only the faithful Persians remain loyal to Ormuzd, fighting under his banner of light and confident that in the final day Ormuzd’s wisdom will overcome Ahriman’s malice. In that ultimate victory, Ahriman will be subdued, his darkness will recede, and virtue will restore eternal peace and harmony to the cosmos.

2. **Creation and Order** – Ormuzd creates a benevolent world, endowing humanity with the capacity for virtue and arranging the natural order (planets, seasons, elements).  
3. **Fall of Harmony** – Ahriman’s envy corrupts him, breaking the original harmony (“Ormuzd’s egg”). After this breach, good and evil are inextricably mixed, leading to constant conflict manifested in natural calamities and human suffering.  
4. **Eschatological Hope** – The text promises a future epoch in which Ormuzd’s wisdom will finally dominate, Ahriman will be defeated, and universal peace and harmony will be restored.

### 1. Main Argument  

1. **Persian martial deficiency** – The author argues that, despite their “civilisation” and “corruption,” the Persians never developed the martial independence, discipline and strategic skill that the northern barbarians (especially the Germans) possessed.  
2. **Structural causes of Persian weakness** – Persian armies relied on sheer numbers, on the luxury‑laden presence of the monarch and his court, and on a lack of professional fortification‑building or disciplined infantry tactics. Their cavalry, while impressive in raw skill, was not organised for the “impending cloud” of coordinated, rapid charges that could threaten Rome.  
3. **Contrast with the Germanic peoples** – By contrast, the Germans are portrayed as “the most civilised nations of modern Europe,” bearing the original principles of European law and manners. Their “primitive simplicity” and “rude institutions” are, in the author’s view, the true source of later European strength.  
4. **Link to the fall of Rome** – Because the eastern Roman provinces faced a “less effective” Persian cavalry, and because the western empire was eventually overthrown by the more martial Germans, the author suggests a causal connection: Persian weakness (and the luxury‑driven decadence of its court) contributed to the decline and eventual fall of the Roman Empire.  

> **In short:** Persians lacked the martial discipline and independence that made the northern barbarians (especially the Germans) successful conquerors; this deficiency, together with the decadent Persian court, helped precipitate Rome’s decline.

| **Formal, academic tone** | Addresses a learned audience; emphasizes objectivity through balanced presentation of evidence. |
| **Parallelism & antithesis** (e.g., “more to their numbers **than** to their courage; more to their courage **than** to their discipline”) | Highlights the author’s claim that Persians were caught between a reliance on quantity and a lack of true martial virtue. |
| **Contrastive juxtaposition** (Persian decadence vs. Germanic vigor) | Creates a stark moral‑political polarity that underpins the argument. |
| **Hyperbolic adjectives** (“most skilful horsemen,” “impending cloud”) | Reinforces the author’s dramatic assessment of Persian military potential (and, by extension, its insufficiency). |
| **Use of footnote numbers** (54‑58) | Signals a meticulous editorial apparatus; the reader is guided to external sources that “prove” each claim. |
| **Didactic, almost pedagogical voice** (“We shall occasionally mention… we shall therefore content ourselves with observing…”) | Positions the text as a teaching tool for future scholars, encouraging repeated examination of the same points. |

Overall, the passage is a **didactic, source‑heavy essay** that uses classical authority and rhetorical contrast to persuade the reader that Persian military shortcomings were a key factor in Rome’s decline, while simultaneously elevating the Germanic peoples as the true bearers of European civilization.

1. **19th‑century historiography of the “Barbarian Invasions”** – Scholars such as Edward Gibbon (later) and contemporary German historians were already framing the fall of Rome as the result of “barbarian” (Germanic) invasions. **1. Main Argument**

The passage is a sustained defence of Edward Gibbon’s *History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire* as a work of supreme historiographical art.  
The reviewer first sketches a **theoretical ideal of unity**: a “sublime Gothic architecture” in which the most disparate episodes—military campaigns, theological controversies, legal reforms—are subordinated to a single, dominant idea – the inexorable decay of Rome. He argues that Gibbon achieves this unity not by simple chronology but by arranging facts “according to their moral or political connection,” marking periods of gradual decline, and showing how religious or civil reforms, whether rapid or slow, fit into a single narrative of Roman corruption.

The reviewer then **contrasts Gibbon with his predecessors**—Tillemont and Le Beau—who “adhere, almost entirely, to chronological order.” The consequence of this method, he claims, is a reader who must constantly “break off, and resume the thread of six or eight wars…to suspend the operations of a military expedition for a court intrigue…and the same page places us in the middle of a campaign against the barbarians, and in the depths of the Monophysite controversy.” In other words, chronological narrative produces fragmentation; Gibbon’s thematic arrangement produces a coherent, “compressed and receding line” that lets the reader see the “real relation of those kingdoms to the empire” even as the political map disintegrates.

The reviewer acknowledges that the **magnificence of Gibbon’s design is impressive**, but he insists that “the amplitude, the magnificence, or the harmony of design … are, though imposing, yet unworthy claims on our admiration, unless the details are filled up with correctness and accuracy.” He notes that Gibbon has been “severely tried” on the point of factual precision—by theological zealots, literary rivals, and “the mean and invidious vanity which delights in detecting errors in writers of established fame.” He then cites a series of learned critics (philosophers of finance, chronologists, theologians, jurists, Orientalists, modern crusade‑scholars) who point out omissions, false or imperfect views, and occasional misquotations, but who nevertheless take Gibbon’s researches and philosophical discrimination as indispensable.

Finally, the passage records a personal conversion: after a first, superficial reading the reviewer found “errors…sufficiently important…to make me believe that they had been written with extreme negligence” and even a “tinge of partiality…misrepresentation.” A second, more patient reading, however, shows that while Gibbon indeed errs and shows bias, these faults do not overturn his overall achievement. The reviewer concludes that “his book, in spite of its faults, will always be a noble work—and that we may correct his errors and combat his prejudices, without ceasing to admit that few men have combined…at least in a manner so complete and so well regulated the necessary qualifications for a writer of history.”

In short, the argument is:

*Gibbon’s genius lies in his ability to impose a single, overarching idea on a vast, chaotic mass of material, thereby producing a unified, thematic narrative of Rome’s decay. This narrative superiority, however brilliant, must be judged alongside rigorous factual work; Gibbon’s occasional inaccuracies and biases do not invalidate his achievement, and his method remains the model for modern historical writing.*

But this admirable skill in selecting and giving       prominence to the points which are of real weight and       importance—this distribution of light and shade—though perhaps it       may occasionally betray him into vague and imperfect statements,       is one of the highest excellencies of Gibbon’s historic manner.       It is the more striking, when we pass from the works of his chief       authorities, where, after laboring through long, minute, and       wearisome descriptions of the accessary and subordinate       circumstances, a single unmarked and undistinguished sentence,       which we may overlook from the inattention of fatigue, contains       the great moral and political result.

Gibbon’s method of arrangement, though on the whole most       favorable to the clear comprehension of the events, leads       likewise to apparent inaccuracy. That which we expect to find in       one part is reserved for another. The estimate which we are to       form, depends on the accurate balance of statements in remote       parts of the work; and we have sometimes to correct and modify       opinions, formed from one chapter by those of another. Yet, on       the other hand, it is astonishing how rarely we detect       contradiction; the mind of the author has already harmonized the       whole result to truth and probability; the general impression is       almost invariably the same. The quotations of Gibbon have       likewise been called in question;—I have, _in general_, been more       inclined to admire their exactitude, than to complain of their       indistinctness, or incompleteness. Where they are imperfect, it       is commonly from the study of brevity, and rather from the desire       of compressing the substance of his notes into pointed and       emphatic sentences, than from dishonesty, or uncandid suppression       of truth.

These observations apply more particularly to the accuracy and       fidelity of the historian as to his facts; his inferences, of       course, are more liable to exception. It is almost impossible to       trace the line between unfairness and unfaithfulness; between       intentional misrepresentation and undesigned false coloring. The       relative magnitude and importance of events must, in some       respect, depend upon the mind before which they are presented;       the estimate of character, on the habits and feelings of the       reader. Christians, like M. Guizot and ourselves, will see some       things, and some persons, in a different light from the historian       of the Decline and Fall. We may deplore the bias of his mind; we       may ourselves be on our guard against the danger of being misled,       and be anxious to warn less wary readers against the same perils;       but we must not confound this secret and unconscious departure       from truth, with the deliberate violation of that veracity which       is the only title of an historian to our confidence. Gibbon, it       may be fearlessly asserted, is rarely chargeable even with the       suppression of any material fact, which bears upon individual       character; he may, with apparently invidious hostility, enhance       the errors and crimes, and disparage the virtues of certain       persons; yet, in general, he leaves us the materials for forming       a fairer judgment; and if he is not exempt from his own       prejudices, perhaps we might write _passions_, yet it must be       candidly acknowledged, that his philosophical bigotry is not more       unjust than the theological partialities of those ecclesiastical       writers who were before in undisputed possession of this province       of history.

But on this subject some preliminary caution is necessary, lest       that should be expected from a new edition, which it is       impossible that it should completely accomplish. We must first be       prepared with the only sound preservative against the false       impression likely to be produced by the perusal of Gibbon; and we       must see clearly the real cause of that false impression. The       former of these cautions will be briefly suggested in its proper       place, but it may be as well to state it, here, somewhat more at       length. The art of Gibbon, or at least the unfair impression       produced by his two memorable chapters, consists in his       confounding together, in one indistinguishable mass, the _origin_       and _apostolic_ propagation of the new religion, with its _later_       progress. No argument for the divine authority of Christianity       has been urged with greater force, or traced with higher       eloquence, than that deduced from its primary development,       explicable on no other hypothesis than a heavenly origin, and       from its rapid extension through great part of the Roman empire.       But this argument—one, when confined within reasonable limits, of       unanswerable force—becomes more feeble and disputable in       proportion as it recedes from the birthplace, as it were, of the       religion. The further Christianity advanced, the more causes       purely human were enlisted in its favor; nor can it be doubted       that those developed with such artful exclusiveness by Gibbon did       concur most essentially to its establishment. It is in the       Christian dispensation, as in the material world. In both it is       as the great First Cause, that the Deity is most undeniably       manifest. When once launched in regular motion upon the bosom of       space, and endowed with all their properties and relations of       weight and mutual attraction, the heavenly bodies appear to       pursue their courses according to secondary laws, which account       for all their sublime regularity. So Christianity proclaims its       Divine Author chiefly in its first origin and development. When       it had once received its impulse from above—when it had once been       infused into the minds of its first teachers—when it had gained       full possession of the reason and affections of the favored       few—it _might be_—and to the Protestant, the rationa Christian,       it is impossible to define _when_ it really _was_—left to make       its way by its native force, under the ordinary secret agencies       of all-ruling Providence. The main question, the _divine origin       of the religion_, was dexterously eluded, or speciously conceded       by Gibbon; his plan enabled him to commence his account, in most       parts, _below the apostolic times;_ and it was only by the       strength of the dark coloring with which he brought out the       failings and the follies of the succeeding ages, that a shadow of       doubt and suspicion was thrown back upon the primitive period of       Christianity.

“The theologian,” says Gibbon, “may indulge the pleasing task of       describing religion as she descended from heaven, arrayed in her       native purity; a more melancholy duty is imposed upon the       historian:—he must discover the inevitable mixture of error and       corruption which she contracted in a long residence upon earth       among a weak and degenerate race of beings.” Divest this passage       of the latent sarcasm betrayed by the subsequent tone of the       whole disquisition, and it might commence a Christian history       written in the most Christian spirit of candor. But as the       historian, by seeming to respect, yet by dexterously confounding       the limits of the sacred land, contrived to insinuate that it was       an Utopia which had no existence but in the imagination of the       theologian—as he _suggested_ rather than affirmed that the days       of Christian purity were a kind of poetic golden age;—so the       theologian, by venturing too far into the domain of the       historian, has been perpetually obliged to contest points on       which he had little chance of victory—to deny facts established       on unshaken evidence—and thence, to retire, if not with the shame       of defeat, yet with but doubtful and imperfect success. Paley,       with his intuitive sagacity, saw through the difficulty of       answering Gibbon by the ordinary arts of controversy; his       emphatic sentence, “Who can refute a sneer?” contains as much       truth as point. But full and pregnant as this phrase is, it is       not quite the whole truth; it is the tone in which the progress       of Christianity is traced, in _comparison_ with the rest of the       splendid and prodigally ornamented work, which is the radical       defect in the “Decline and Fall.” Christianity alone receives no       embellishment from the magic of Gibbon’s language; his       imagination is dead to its moral dignity; it is kept down by a       general zone of jealous disparagement, or neutralized by a       painfully elaborate exposition of its darker and degenerate       periods. There are occasions, indeed, when its pure and exalted       humanity, when its manifestly beneficial influence, can compel       even him, as it were, to fairness, and kindle his unguarded       eloquence to its usual fervor; but, in general, he soon relapses       into a frigid apathy; _affects_ an ostentatiously severe       impartiality; notes all the faults of Christians in every age       with bitter and almost malignant sarcasm; reluctantly, and with       exception and reservation, admits their claim to admiration. This       inextricable bias appears even to influence his manner of       composition. While all the other assailants of the Roman empire,       whether warlike or religious, the Goth, the Hun, the Arab, the       Tartar, Alaric and Attila, Mahomet, and Zengis, and Tamerlane,       are each introduced upon the scene almost with dramatic       animation—their progress related in a full, complete, and       unbroken narrative—the triumph of Christianity alone takes the       form of a cold and critical disquisition. The successes of       barbarous energy and brute force call forth all the consummate       skill of composition; while the moral triumphs of Christian       benevolence—the tranquil heroism of endurance, the blameless       purity, the contempt of guilty fame and of honors destructive to       the human race, which, had they assumed the proud name of       philosophy, would have been blazoned in his brightest words,       because they own religion as their principle—sink into narrow       asceticism. The _glories_ of Christianity, in short, touch on no       chord in the heart of the writer; his imagination remains       unkindled; his words, though they maintain their stately and       measured march, have become cool, argumentative, and inanimate.       Who would obscure one hue of that gorgeous coloring in which       Gibbon has invested the dying forms of Paganism, or darken one       paragraph in his splendid view of the rise and progress of       Mahometanism? But who would not have wished that the same equal       justice had been done to Christianity; that its real character       and deeply penetrating influence had been traced with the same       philosophical sagacity, and represented with more sober, as would       become its quiet course, and perhaps less picturesque, but still       with lively and attractive, descriptiveness? He might have thrown       aside, with the same scorn, the mass of ecclesiastical fiction       which envelops the early history of the church, stripped off the       legendary romance, and brought out the facts in their primitive       nakedness and simplicity—if he had but allowed those facts the       benefit of the glowing eloquence which he denied to them alone.       He might have annihilated the whole fabric of post-apostolic       miracles, if he had left uninjured by sarcastic insinuation those       of the New Testament; he might have cashiered, with Dodwell, the       whole host of martyrs, which owe their existence to the prodigal       invention of later days, had he but bestowed fair room, and dwelt       with his ordinary energy on the sufferings of the genuine       witnesses to the truth of Christianity, the Polycarps, or the       martyrs of Vienne. And indeed, if, after all, the view of the       early progress of Christianity be melancholy and humiliating we       must beware lest we charge the whole of this on the infidelity of       the historian. It is idle, it is disingenuous, to deny or to       dissemble the early depravations of Christianity, its gradual but       rapid departure from its primitive simplicity and purity, still       more, from its spirit of universal love. It may be no unsalutary       lesson to the Christian world, that this silent, this       unavoidable, perhaps, yet fatal change shall have been drawn by       an impartial, or even an hostile hand. The Christianity of every       age may take warning, lest by its own narrow views, its want of       wisdom, and its want of charity, it give the same advantage to       the future unfriendly historian, and disparage the cause of true       religion.

The design of the present edition is partly corrective, partly       supplementary: corrective, by notes, which point out (it is       hoped, in a perfectly candid and dispassionate spirit with no       desire but to establish the truth) such inaccuracies or       misstatements as may have been detected, particularly with regard       to Christianity; and which thus, with the previous caution, may       counteract to a considerable extent the unfair and unfavorable       impression created against rational religion: supplementary, by       adding such additional information as the editor’s reading may       have been able to furnish, from original documents or books, not       accessible at the time when Gibbon wrote.

The chief works from which the editor has derived his materials       are, I. The French translation, with notes by M. Guizot; 2d       edition, Paris, 1828. The editor has translated almost all the       notes of M. Guizot. Where he has not altogether agreed with him,       his respect for the learning and judgment of that writer has, in       general, induced him to retain the statement from which he has       ventured to differ, with the grounds on which he formed his own       opinion. In the notes on Christianity, he has retained all those       of M. Guizot, with his own, from the conviction, that on such a       subject, to many, the authority of a French statesman, a       Protestant, and a rational and sincere Christian, would appear       more independent and unbiassed, and therefore be more commanding,       than that of an English clergyman.

IV. The editor has consulted the various answers made to Gibbon       on the first appearance of his work; he must confess, with little       profit. They were, in general, hastily compiled by inferior and       now forgotten writers, with the exception of Bishop Watson, whose       able apology is rather a general argument, than an examination of       misstatements. The name of Milner stands higher with a certain       class of readers, but will not carry much weight with the severe       investigator of history.

V. Some few classical works and fragments have come to light,       since the appearance of Gibbon’s History, and have been noticed       in their respective places; and much use has been made, in the       latter volumes particularly, of the increase to our stores of       Oriental literature. The editor cannot, indeed, pretend to have       followed his author, in these gleanings, over the whole vast       field of his inquiries; he may have overlooked or may not have       been able to command some works, which might have thrown still       further light on these subjects; but he trusts that what he has       adduced will be of use to the student of historic truth.

The passage also seeks to reassure his readers that his forthcoming historical work will be grounded in truth, that his personal reflections do not signal a permanent farewell, and that the pursuit of knowledge remains his most compelling motive.

The author adopts a three‑part rhetorical strategy that mirrors the structure of his text:

1. **Personal‑Patronage Appeal** – He begins with a warm, nostalgic portrait of his private life (the lakes of Lausanne, “a mild government, amidst a beauteous landscape”) and then pivots to a public‑political appeal, emphasizing his pride in being an Englishman and the honour of “the approbation of that country.”  This moves the audience from intimacy to civic pride, establishing an ethos of a loyal, patriotic writer.

2. **Logical‑Pragmatic Reasoning** – He presents a series of practical concerns (the fatigue of publishing six quartos, the risk of losing readership, the comparative loss of a “regular work”) followed by a philosophical balancing act (“the motives of action or silence are now equally balanced”). 3. **Moral‑Patriotic Persuasion** – The passage ends with a confident assertion that “the liberty and variety of study” outweigh the “design and composition of a regular work,” thereby appealing to pathos: the author frames his labour as a civic duty and a source of personal fulfillment.

The overall style is reflective yet assertive, combining the private tone of a gentleman’s journal with the public, scholarly tone of an Enlightenment historian.

Nine centuries of war had gradually introduced into the service       many alterations and improvements. The legions, as they are       described by Polybius, 41 in the time of the Punic wars, differed       very materially from those which achieved the victories of Cæsar,       or defended the monarchy of Hadrian and the Antonines. The       constitution of the Imperial legion may be described in a few       words. 42 The heavy-armed infantry, which composed its principal       strength, 43 was divided into ten cohorts, and fifty-five       companies, under the orders of a correspondent number of tribunes       and centurions. The first cohort, which always claimed the post       of honor and the custody of the eagle, was formed of eleven       hundred and five soldiers, the most approved for valor and       fidelity. The remaining nine cohorts consisted each of five       hundred and fifty-five; and the whole body of legionary infantry       amounted to six thousand one hundred men. Their arms were       uniform, and admirably adapted to the nature of their service: an       open helmet, with a lofty crest; a breastplate, or coat of mail;       greaves on their legs, and an ample buckler on their left arm.       The buckler was of an oblong and concave figure, four feet in       length, and two and a half in breadth, framed of a light wood,       covered with a bull’s hide, and strongly guarded with plates of       brass. Besides a lighter spear, the legionary soldier grasped in       his right hand the formidable _pilum_, a ponderous javelin, whose       utmost length was about six feet, and which was terminated by a       massy triangular point of steel of eighteen inches. 44 This       instrument was indeed much inferior to our modern fire-arms;       since it was exhausted by a single discharge, at the distance of       only ten or twelve paces. As soon as the Roman had darted his       _pilum_, he drew his sword, and rushed forwards to close with the       enemy. His sword was a short well-tempered Spanish blade, that       carried a double edge, and was alike suited to the purpose of       striking or of pushing; but the soldier was always instructed to       prefer the latter use of his weapon, as his own body remained       less exposed, whilst he inflicted a more dangerous wound on his       adversary. 45 The legion was usually drawn up eight deep; and the       regular distance of three feet was left between the files as well       as ranks. 46 A body of troops, habituated to preserve this open       order, in a long front and a rapid charge, found themselves       prepared to execute every disposition which the circumstances of       war, or the skill of their leader, might suggest. The strength of the phalanx depended on       sixteen ranks of long pikes, wedged together in the closest       array. 48 But it was soon discovered by reflection, as well as by       the event, that the strength of the phalanx was unable to contend       with the activity of the legion. 49

The entire establishment formed a       regiment, if we may use the modern expression, of seven hundred       and twenty-six horse, naturally connected with its respective       legion, but occasionally separated to act in the line, and to       compose a part of the wings of the army. 50 The cavalry of the       emperors was no longer composed, like that of the ancient       republic, of the noblest youths of Rome and Italy, who, by       performing their military service on horseback, prepared       themselves for the offices of senator and consul; and solicited,       by deeds of valor, the future suffrages of their countrymen. 51       Since the alteration of manners and government, the most wealthy       of the equestrian order were engaged in the administration of       justice, and of the revenue; 52 and whenever they embraced the       profession of arms, they were immediately intrusted with a troop       of horse, or a cohort of foot. 53 Trajan and Hadrian formed their       cavalry from the same provinces, and the same class of their       subjects, which recruited the ranks of the legion. This temporal cue is a classic rhetorical device: by situating the narrative in a moment of loss and subsequent subjugation, the author foregrounds Rome’s civilizing mission.

The author’s **enumerative style** is evident in the catalogue of peoples and regions (“thirty tribes… the Belgæ… the Brigantes… the Silures… the Iceni”; “Rhætia, Noricum, Pannonia, Dalmatia, Dacia, Mæsia, Thrace, Macedonia, and Greece”). Such lists create a sense of completeness and authority; the repetition of “province” and “region” reinforces the imperial administrative schema. Moreover, the use of **parallelism** – “the river… flows above thirteen hundred miles… and is, at length, through six mouths, received into the Euxine” – underscores the grandeur of the Danube while also echoing the classical description of its power.

The passage is heavily laced with **classical allusions** that lend it an aura of scholarly gravitas. References to “the columns of Hercules,” “the Tagus,” “Hercules,” and the mythic cities of Greece (Thebes, Argos, Sparta, Athens) function as signposts for the learned reader and as a rhetorical bridge between the ancient world and the contemporary political map. By invoking these names, the author subtly affirms the continuity of Roman cultural influence, positioning the empire as the inheritor and transmitter of Greek civilization (“Italy was indebted for the first rudiments of civilized life” to the Etruscans).

The frequent use of **impersonal third‑person constructions** (“the provinces of the Danube soon acquired the general appellation of Illyricum”) also contributes to an objective tone, allowing the author to present facts as inevitable outcomes rather than subjective judgments.

The author’s **evaluative adjectives**—“the most warlike of the empire,” “savage independence,” “flourishing colonies”—reveal a normative stance that places Rome at the centre of a moral hierarchy. By labeling the Danube frontier “the most warlike” and the Illyrian peoples “fierce,” the writer not only describes but also justifies Roman dominance as a necessary civilizing force. This moral framing aligns with 18th‑century Enlightenment historiography, which often portrayed empire as a conduit for order and refinement.

The geographers of antiquity have frequently hesitated to what       portion of the globe they should ascribe Egypt. 85 By its       situation that celebrated kingdom is included within the immense       peninsula of Africa; but it is accessible only on the side of       Asia, whose revolutions, in almost every period of history, Egypt       has humbly obeyed. A Roman præfect was seated on the splendid       throne of the Ptolemies; and the iron sceptre of the Mamelukes is       now in the hands of a Turkish pacha. The Nile flows down the       country, above five hundred miles from the tropic of Cancer to       the Mediterranean, and marks on either side the extent of       fertility by the measure of its inundations. Cyrene, situate       towards the west, and along the sea-coast, was first a Greek       colony, afterwards a province of Egypt, and is now lost in the       desert of Barca. 851

851 (return) [ The French editor has a long and unnecessary note       on the History of Cyrene. For the present state of that coast and       country, the volume of Captain Beechey is full of interesting       details. Egypt, now an independent and improving kingdom,       appears, under the enterprising rule of Mahommed Ali, likely to       revenge its former oppression upon the decrepit power of the       Turkish empire.—M.—This note was written in 1838. The future       destiny of Egypt is an important problem, only to be solved by       time. This observation will also apply to the new French colony       in Algiers.—M. 1845.]

From Cyrene to the ocean, the coast of Africa extends above       fifteen hundred miles; yet so closely is it pressed between the       Mediterranean and the Sahara, or sandy desert, that its breadth       seldom exceeds fourscore or a hundred miles. The eastern division       was considered by the Romans as the more peculiar and proper       province of Africa. Till the arrival of the Phœnician colonies,       that fertile country was inhabited by the Libyans, the most       savage of mankind. Under the immediate jurisdiction of Carthage,       it became the centre of commerce and empire; but the republic of       Carthage is now degenerated into the feeble and disorderly states       of Tripoli and Tunis. The military government of Algiers       oppresses the wide extent of Numidia, as it was once united under       Massinissa and Jugurtha; but in the time of Augustus, the limits       of Numidia were contracted; and, at least, two thirds of the       country acquiesced in the name of Mauritania, with the epithet of       Cæsariensis. The genuine Mauritania, or country of the Moors,       which, from the ancient city of Tingi, or Tangier, was       distinguished by the appellation of Tingitana, is represented by       the modern kingdom of Fez. Salle, on the Ocean, so infamous at       present for its piratical depredations, was noticed by the       Romans, as the extreme object of their power, and almost of their       geography. A city of their foundation may still be discovered       near Mequinez, the residence of the barbarian whom we condescend       to style the Emperor of Morocco; but it does not appear, that his       more southern dominions, Morocco itself, and Segelmessa, were       ever comprehended within the Roman province. The western parts of       Africa are intersected by the branches of Mount Atlas, a name so       idly celebrated by the fancy of poets; 86 but which is now       diffused over the immense ocean that rolls between the ancient       and the new continent. 87

86 (return) [ The long range, moderate height, and gentle       declivity of Mount Atlas, (see Shaw’s Travels, p. 5,) are very       unlike a solitary mountain which rears its head into the clouds,       and seems to support the heavens. The peak of Teneriff, on the       contrary, rises a league and a half above the surface of the sea;       and, as it was frequently visited by the Phœnicians, might engage       the notice of the Greek poets. See Buffon, Histoire Naturelle,       tom. i. p. 312. Histoire des Voyages, tom. ii.]

Having now finished the circuit of the Roman empire, we may       observe, that Africa is divided from Spain by a narrow strait of       about twelve miles, through which the Atlantic flows into the       Mediterranean. The columns of Hercules, so famous among the       ancients, were two mountains which seemed to have been torn       asunder by some convulsion of the elements; and at the foot of       the European mountain, the fortress of Gibraltar is now seated.       The whole extent of the Mediterranean Sea, its coasts and its       islands, were comprised within the Roman dominion. Of the larger       islands, the two Baleares, which derive their name of Majorca and       Minorca from their respective size, are subject at present, the       former to Spain, the latter to Great Britain. 871 It is easier to       deplore the fate, than to describe the actual condition, of       Corsica. 872 Two Italian sovereigns assume a regal title from       Sardinia and Sicily. Crete, or Candia, with Cyprus, and most of       the smaller islands of Greece and Asia, have been subdued by the       Turkish arms, whilst the little rock of Malta defies their power,       and has emerged, under the government of its military Order, into       fame and opulence. 873

This long enumeration of provinces, whose broken fragments have       formed so many powerful kingdoms, might almost induce us to       forgive the vanity or ignorance of the ancients. Dazzled with the       extensive sway, the irresistible strength, and the real or       affected moderation of the emperors, they permitted themselves to       despise, and sometimes to forget, the outlying countries which       had been left in the enjoyment of a barbarous independence; and       they gradually usurped the license of confounding the Roman       monarchy with the globe of the earth. 88 But the temper, as well       as knowledge, of a modern historian, require a more sober and       accurate language. The passage argues that the Roman Empire’s expansion was never merely a military conquest; it was accompanied by a systematic programme of settlement, legal integration and cultural assimilation that produced a durable “Romanisation” of the western provinces while leaving a distinct Greek‑language and cultural sphere in the east.  The author builds this claim on three inter‑locking strands:

1. **Political‑institutional privileges** – cities retained a degree of self‑government (the “right of Latium”) and, after the emperor’s favour, could be granted Roman citizenship, thereby creating a class of provincial elites who identified with Rome.  The passage cites Tacitus and Walther to show that these privileges were granted at the emperor’s whim and that they circulated among the most prominent families.

2. **Demographic and economic colonisation** – after the legions became permanent, the empire was repopulated by soldiers and their veterans, who settled in the most fertile lands and founded both civil and military colonies.  These colonies acted as “perfect representations of their great parent,” quickly earning the friendship of the natives and spreading Roman law, language and customs.  By the time of Hadrian, municipal cities had essentially caught up with the colonies in status.

3. **Cultural‑linguistic diffusion** – the Romans deliberately spread Latin as the language of administration, law and education.  The ancient Italian dialects disappear, while the east is slower to adopt Latin; the “western countries were civilized by the same hands which subdued them,” and the Latin of Virgil and Cicero becomes the lingua‑franca of Africa, Spain, Gaul, Britain and Pannonia.  Conversely, the Greek east retained its own linguistic prestige, displaying a mixture of vanity, taste and resistance that kept Greek culture alive despite Roman political dominance.

In sum, the text presents Romanisation as a two‑track process: a rapid, state‑driven diffusion of Roman law and Latin in the West, and a more gradual, culturally resistant continuation of Greek traditions in the East.  The argument is reinforced by a long chronological sweep—from the Mithridatic massacre (80 000 Romans) through the permanent legions of Augustus, the Hadrianic building programme, to the Antonine era—showing that the policy was long‑standing and cumulative.

“Upon establishing despotic government in the Roman empire,       domestic tyranny rose, in a short time, to an astonishing height.       In that rank soil, every vice, which power nourishes in the       great, or oppression engenders in the mean, thrived and grew up       apace. * * * It is not the authority of any single detached       precept in the gospel, but the spirit and genius of the Christian       religion, more powerful than any particular command, which hath       abolished the practice of slavery throughout the world. Is it in such a       situation, with such notions, that the sentiments of nature       unfold themselves, or habits of education become mild and       peaceful? Since the publication of my first annotated edition of Gibbon,       the subject of the population of the Roman empire has been       investigated by two writers of great industry and learning; Mons.       Dureau de la Malle, in his Economie Politique des Romains, liv.       ii. c. 1. to 8, and M. Zumpt, in a dissertation printed in the       Transactions of the Berlin Academy, 1840. M. Dureau de la Malle       confines his inquiry almost entirely to the city of Rome, and       Roman Italy. Zumpt examines at greater length the axiom, which he       supposes to have been assumed by Gibbon as unquestionable, “that       Italy and the Roman world was never so populous as in the time of       the Antonines.” Though this probably was Gibbon’s opinion, he has       not stated it so peremptorily as asserted by Mr. Zumpt. It had       before been expressly laid down by Hume, and his statement was       controverted by Wallace and by Malthus. Gibbon says (p. 84) that       there is no reason to believe the country (of Italy) less       populous in the age of the Antonines, than in that of Romulus;       and Zumpt acknowledges that we have no satisfactory knowledge of       the state of Italy at that early age. Zumpt, in my opinion with       some reason, takes the period just before the first Punic war, as       that in which Roman Italy (all south of the Rubicon) was most       populous. From that time, the numbers began to diminish, at first       from the enormous waste of life out of the free population in the       foreign, and afterwards in the civil wars; from the cultivation       of the soil by slaves; towards the close of the republic, from       the repugnance to marriage, which resisted alike the dread of       legal punishment and the offer of legal immunity and privilege;       and from the depravity of manners, which interfered with the       procreation, the birth, and the rearing of children. The       arguments and the authorities of Zumpt are equally conclusive as       to the decline of population in Greece. Still the details, which       he himself adduces as to the prosperity and populousness of Asia       Minor, and the whole of the Roman East, with the advancement of       the European provinces, especially Gaul, Spain, and Britain, in       civilization, and therefore in populousness, (for I have no       confidence in the vast numbers sometimes assigned to the       barbarous inhabitants of these countries,) may, I think, fairly       compensate for any deduction to be made from Gibbon’s general       estimate on account of Greece and Italy. Gibbon himself       acknowledges his own estimate to be vague and conjectural; and I       may venture to recommend the dissertation of Zumpt as deserving       respectful consideration.—M 1815.]

Domestic peace and union were the natural consequences of the       moderate and comprehensive policy embraced by the Romans. If we       turn our eyes towards the monarchies of Asia, we shall behold       despotism in the centre, and weakness in the extremities; the       collection of the revenue, or the administration of justice,       enforced by the presence of an army; hostile barbarians       established in the heart of the country, hereditary satraps       usurping the dominion of the provinces, and subjects inclined to       rebellion, though incapable of freedom. But the obedience of the       Roman world was uniform, voluntary, and permanent. The vanquished       nations, blended into one great people, resigned the hope, nay,       even the wish, of resuming their independence, and scarcely       considered their own existence as distinct from the existence of       Rome. The established authority of the emperors pervaded without       an effort the wide extent of their dominions, and was exercised       with the same facility on the banks of the Thames, or of the       Nile, as on those of the Tyber. The legions were destined to       serve against the public enemy, and the civil magistrate seldom       required the aid of a military force. 63 In this state of general       security, the leisure, as well as opulence, both of the prince       and people, were devoted to improve and to adorn the Roman       empire.

Among the innumerable monuments of architecture constructed by       the Romans, how many have escaped the notice of history, how few       have resisted the ravages of time and barbarism! And yet, even       the majestic ruins that are still scattered over Italy and the       provinces, would be sufficient to prove that those countries were       once the seat of a polite and powerful empire. Their greatness       alone, or their beauty, might deserve our attention: but they are       rendered more interesting, by two important circumstances, which       connect the agreeable history of the arts with the more useful       history of human manners. Many of those works were erected at       private expense, and almost all were intended for public benefit.

It is natural to suppose that the greatest number, as well as the       most considerable of the Roman edifices, were raised by the       emperors, who possessed so unbounded a command both of men and       money. Augustus was accustomed to boast that he had found his       capital of brick, and that he had left it of marble. 64 The       strict economy of Vespasian was the source of his magnificence.       The works of Trajan bear the stamp of his genius. The public       monuments with which Hadrian adorned every province of the       empire, were executed not only by his orders, but under his       immediate inspection. He was himself an artist; and he loved the       arts, as they conduced to the glory of the monarch. They were       encouraged by the Antonines, as they contributed to the happiness       of the people. But if the emperors were the first, they were not       the only architects of their dominions. The argument is that these material facts—urban density, road density, and the imperial post system—were the primary mechanisms by which Rome bound its distant provinces together, facilitated the movement of legions, and projected Roman authority.  Implicitly, the author also seeks to correct earlier, often exaggerated, city‑counts (e.g. Josephus’s 1 197 Italian cities) by appealing to a mixture of ancient testimony and modern travellers’ observations, thereby presenting a more reliable picture of the empire’s scale.

**2. Rhetorical style**

The text is a textbook example of 19th‑century antiquarian scholarship: it is highly systematic, data‑driven and heavily sourced.  Its structure (I, II, III, IV) mirrors a classical rhetorical progression—statement of fact, comparison, and conclusion—while the language is deliberately formal and often Latinate (“the spirit of improvement”, “the proper Asia alone contained five hundred populous cities”). The passage belongs to the wave of Roman‑studies that gathered momentum in the early‑ to mid‑19th century. The demand for luxury goods created a market that paid the “diligent mechanic” and “skilful artist” a voluntary tax (i.e., a share of the estate’s produce).  In turn, land‑owners, motivated by personal interest, improved their estates so they could purchase more luxury items.  This virtuous circle kept the provincial economies productive and, by feeding the state’s tax base, helped the Roman political machine stay active.  

2. **Correcting unequal property** – In a society where most people own little land, luxury purchases provided a way for the industrious but land‑less to obtain income, thereby “correcting the unequal distribution of property.”  

3. **Trade‑deficit problem** – The empire’s luxury appetite, however, forced it to draw raw materials and finished goods from far‑flung regions (Scythia, the Baltic, Arabia, India).  The most valuable imports were silk, pearls, precious stones, and exotic aromatics.  Although the voyages from Myos‑Hormos (≈120 ships a year) yielded spectacular profits, those profits accrued to a few individuals at the expense of the public purse; the state lost silver—especially in the purchase of foreign female ornaments—estimated at > £800 000 per annum.  

4. **Silver‑production offset** – Nevertheless, the proportion of gold to silver in the Roman economy rose from the time of Pliny (c. 77 CE) to Constantine, showing that **silver was becoming more abundant** and that the mines could meet the demand generated by luxury trade.  Thus the empire’s wealth was not exhausted despite the outward flow of silver.  

5. **Overall assessment** – While moralists (ancient and modern) condemn luxury as a sign of vice, the author concludes that, under the Roman system, it was a necessary—and largely beneficial—force that helped sustain prosperity, cultural flourishing, and internal peace.

**Main rhetorical style**

The passage blends several rhetorical modes:

| Element | How it is used | Effect |
|---------|----------------|--------|
| **Moral condemnation** (e.g., “luxury… have been severely arraigned”) | Classical moralising tradition (Stoic, Christian) | Sets up a contrast that makes the later economic argument more persuasive. |
| **Didactic exposition** (definition of agriculture as foundation of manufactures, description of market mechanisms) | Straight‑forward, systematic analysis | Gives the argument a scholarly, “scientific” tone. |
| **Enumeration & listing** (furs from Scythia, amber from the Baltic, silk, pearls, aromatics) | Concrete examples that illustrate abstract points | Makes the economic case vivid and memorable. |
| **Antithesis** (necessaries vs. superfluities; “if all possessed the necessaries… none the superfluities”) | Highlights the moral‑economic tension | Drives home the author’s central claim that luxury, though superfluous, serves a necessary social function. |
| **Elevated diction & metaphor** (provinces “exhausted of wealth,” “impressive splendor of the cities… cultivated and adorned like an immense garden”) | Classical grandeur, “high style” | Reinforces the idea of Rome as a civilising, almost mythic, power. |
| **Use of ancient authorities** (Eumenius, Pliny, Arrian, Gibbon, Wenck) | Authority‑borrowing (ethos) | Lends credibility and a scholarly veneer to the economic‑moral thesis. |
| **Balanced, measured tone** (acknowledges both benefits and drawbacks) | Moderation, “middle‑ground” approach | Avoids simplistic moralising and makes the economic argument more defensible. |

Overall, the style is **polemical‑didactic**: it argues a controversial point (that luxury is indispensable) while simultaneously presenting the moral objections, using extensive classical references and vivid imagery to persuade the reader.

> **Footnote 1051** – “Certainly not the only one. The Indians were not so contented with regard to foreign productions.
