**Source citations for footnote 1051**

| Reference | Details |
|-----------|---------|
| **Arrian, *Periplus Maris Erythræi*** (see Hudson, *Geographia Mineralis* i. p. 27) | Provides the list of European wares (wine, metals, coral, glass, clothing) that Indians imported in exchange for their own products (spices, silk, pearls, etc.). |

The       former were attended by lictors, the latter by soldiers. 105 A       law was passed, that wherever the emperor was present, his       extraordinary commission should supersede the ordinary       jurisdiction of the governor; a custom was introduced, that the       new conquests belonged to the imperial portion; and it was soon       discovered that the authority of the _Prince_, the favorite       epithet of Augustus, was the same in every part of the empire.

The       lieutenants of the emperor, who were called Proprætors, whether       they had been prætors or consuls, were attended by six lictors;       those who had the right of the sword, (of life and death over the       soldiers.—M.) bore the military habit (paludamentum) and the       sword. The provinces of Africa and Asia were       only given to ex-consuls. See, on the Organization of the       Provinces, Dion, liii. 12, 16 Strabo, xvii 840.—W]

In return for this imaginary concession, Augustus obtained an       important privilege, which rendered him master of Rome and Italy.       By a dangerous exception to the ancient maxims, he was authorized       to preserve his military command, supported by a numerous body of       guards, even in time of peace, and in the heart of the capital.       His command, indeed, was confined to those citizens who were       engaged in the service by the military oath; but such was the       propensity of the Romans to servitude, that the oath was       voluntarily taken by the magistrates, the senators, and the       equestrian order, till the homage of flattery was insensibly       converted into an annual and solemn protestation of fidelity.

Although Augustus considered a military force as the firmest       foundation, he wisely rejected it, as a very odious instrument of       government. It was more agreeable to his temper, as well as to       his policy, to reign under the venerable names of ancient       magistracy, and artfully to collect, in his own person, all the       scattered rays of civil jurisdiction. With this view, he       permitted the senate to confer upon him, for his life, the powers       of the consular 11 and tribunitian offices, 12 which were, in the       same manner, continued to all his successors. The consuls had       succeeded to the kings of Rome, and represented the dignity of       the state. They superintended the ceremonies of religion, levied       and commanded the legions, gave audience to foreign ambassadors,       and presided in the assemblies both of the senate and people. The       general control of the finances was intrusted to their care; and       though they seldom had leisure to administer justice in person,       they were considered as the supreme guardians of law, equity, and       the public peace. Such was their ordinary jurisdiction; but       whenever the senate empowered the first magistrate to consult the       safety of the commonwealth, he was raised by that decree above       the laws, and exercised, in the defence of liberty, a temporary       despotism. 13 The character of the tribunes was, in every       respect, different from that of the consuls. The appearance of       the former was modest and humble; but their persons were sacred       and inviolable. Their force was suited rather for opposition than       for action. They were instituted to defend the oppressed, to       pardon offences, to arraign the enemies of the people, and, when       they judged it necessary, to stop, by a single word, the whole       machine of government. As long as the republic subsisted, the       dangerous influence, which either the consul or the tribune might       derive from their respective jurisdiction, was diminished by       several important restrictions. Their authority expired with the       year in which they were elected; the former office was divided       between two, the latter among ten persons; and, as both in their       private and public interest they were averse to each other, their       mutual conflicts contributed, for the most part, to strengthen       rather than to destroy the balance of the constitution. 131 But       when the consular and tribunitian powers were united, when they       were vested for life in a single person, when the general of the       army was, at the same time, the minister of the senate and the       representative of the Roman people, it was impossible to resist       the exercise, nor was it easy to define the limits, of his       imperial prerogative.

To these accumulated honors, the policy of Augustus soon added       the splendid as well as important dignities of supreme pontiff,       and of censor. By the former he acquired the management of the       religion, and by the latter a legal inspection over the manners       and fortunes, of the Roman people. The passage argues that the Roman practice of deifying the emperor was never a genuine act of religious devotion but a *policy* of political legitimation. Augustus was the first Roman ruler to adopt this practice, but he did so cautiously: he permitted provincial temples only on the condition that the worship of Rome be paired with his own, and he left the formal apotheosis of the dead emperor to the Senate.  Subsequent emperors—Caligula, Domitian—exploited the same mechanism for personal aggrandizement, while the Antonine “virtuous” line was portrayed as a moral counter‑example.

Two related sub‑arguments are woven through the text:

1. **The Evolution of Imperial Titulature** – The names *Caesar* and *Augustus* did not arise spontaneously; they were political inventions.  *Caesar* became a hereditary, “imperial” designation after Nero, while *Augustus* remained the exclusive honorific of the reigning monarch, later applied to the presumptive heir (the “second person in the state”). 2. **Deification as a Pragmatic Institution, Not a Religious One** – The author stresses that the Senate’s decree of apotheosis was a *legal* act, not a divine proclamation. Thus, the text frames imperial deification as a *policy* that served the regime’s need for legitimacy rather than a genuine cultic devotion.

In sum, the passage contends that Roman imperial deification was a calculated political instrument rooted in earlier monarchic cults, that Augustus inaugurated it with restraint, and that later emperors abused it, while the moral valuation of “virtuous” Antonine rule stands in stark contrast to the “vices” attributed to mythic deities.

His reign       is marked by the rare advantage of furnishing very few materials       for history; which is, indeed, little more than the register of       the crimes, follies, and misfortunes of mankind. He enjoyed       with moderation the conveniences of his fortune, and the innocent       pleasures of society; 44 and the benevolence of his soul       displayed itself in a cheerful serenity of temper.

The virtue of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus was of severer and more       laborious kind. 45 It was the well-earned harvest of many a       learned conference, of many a patient lecture, and many a       midnight lucubration. At the age of twelve years he embraced the       rigid system of the Stoics, which taught him to submit his body       to his mind, his passions to his reason; to consider virtue as       the only good, vice as the only evil, all things external as       things indifferent. 46 His meditations, composed in the tumult of       the camp, are still extant; and he even condescended to give       lessons of philosophy, in a more public manner than was perhaps       consistent with the modesty of sage, or the dignity of an       emperor. 47 But his life was the noblest commentary on the       precepts of Zeno. Even Marcus Antoninus has been called a hypocrite; but the       wildest scepticism never insinuated that Cæsar might probably be       a coward, or Tully a fool. If a man were called to fix the period in the history of the       world, during which the condition of the human race was most       happy and prosperous, he would, without hesitation, name that       which elapsed from the death of Domitian to the accession of       Commodus. The vast extent of the Roman empire was governed by       absolute power, under the guidance of virtue and wisdom. The       armies were restrained by the firm but gentle hand of four       successive emperors, whose characters and authority commanded       involuntary respect. The forms of the civil administration were       carefully preserved by Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, and the Antonines,       who delighted in the image of liberty, and were pleased with       considering themselves as the accountable ministers of the laws.       Such princes deserved the honor of restoring the republic, had       the Romans of their days been capable of enjoying a rational       freedom.

The labors of these monarchs were overpaid by the immense reward       that inseparably waited on their success; by the honest pride of       virtue, and by the exquisite delight of beholding the general       happiness of which they were the authors. A just but melancholy       reflection imbittered, however, the noblest of human enjoyments.       They must often have recollected the instability of a happiness       which depended on the character of single man. The fatal moment       was perhaps approaching, when some licentious youth, or some       jealous tyrant, would abuse, to the destruction, that absolute       power, which they had exerted for the benefit of their people.       The ideal restraints of the senate and the laws might serve to       display the virtues, but could never correct the vices, of the       emperor. The military force was a blind and irresistible       instrument of oppression; and the corruption of Roman manners       would always supply flatterers eager to applaud, and ministers       prepared to serve, the fear or the avarice, the lust or the       cruelty, of their master. The annals of       the emperors exhibit a strong and various picture of human       nature, which we should vainly seek among the mixed and doubtful       characters of modern history. ## 1. Main Argument  

The passage is a **comparative moral‑historical essay** that uses two very different “slave”‑situations—a Persian courtier‑eunuch (the “king’s slave”) and the Roman subject under imperial tyranny—to argue three inter‑related points:

1. **Slavery is universally unjust**, even when it is embedded in a culture that treats the slave with a degree of privilege (Persian “king’s slave”) or when it is mitigated by republican ideals (Roman past).  
2. **Absolute monarchy produces the most pernicious forms of bondage**, because the sovereign’s capricious cruelty can be hidden behind the veneer of legal ownership, while the Roman experience shows how a once‑liberal civic tradition can be perverted into systematic oppression.  
3. **Political fragmentation and the preservation of civic liberty are essential for genuine freedom**; the Roman Empire’s unification turned the world into a “dreary prison” for every subject, whereas a Europe of independent states, bound only by common religion, language and manners, creates “the most beneficial consequences to the liberty of mankind”.

Nothing however, was neglected by       the anxious father, and by the men of virtue and learning whom he       summoned to his assistance, to expand the narrow mind of young       Commodus, to correct his growing vices, and to render him worthy       of the throne for which he was designed. But the power of       instruction is seldom of much efficacy, except in those happy       dispositions where it is almost superfluous. The distasteful       lesson of a grave philosopher was, in a moment, obliterated by       the whisper of a profligate favorite; and Marcus himself blasted       the fruits of this labored education, by admitting his son, at       the age of fourteen or fifteen, to a full participation of the       Imperial power. He lived but four years afterwards: but he lived       long enough to repent a rash measure, which raised the impetuous       youth above the restraint of reason and authority.

Most of the crimes which disturb the internal peace of society,       are produced by the restraints which the necessary but unequal       laws of property have imposed on the appetites of mankind, by       confining to a few the possession of those objects that are       coveted by many. Of all our passions and appetites, the love of       power is of the most imperious and unsociable nature, since the       pride of one man requires the submission of the multitude. In the       tumult of civil discord, the laws of society lose their force,       and their place is seldom supplied by those of humanity. The       ardor of contention, the pride of victory, the despair of       success, the memory of past injuries, and the fear of future       dangers, all contribute to inflame the mind, and to silence the       voice of pity. From such motives almost every page of history has       been stained with civil blood; but these motives will not account       for the unprovoked cruelties of Commodus, who had nothing to wish       and every thing to enjoy. The beloved son of Marcus succeeded to       his father, amidst the acclamations of the senate and armies; 6       and when he ascended the throne, the happy youth saw round him       neither competitor to remove, nor enemies to punish. In this       calm, elevated station, it was surely natural that he should       prefer the love of mankind to their detestation, the mild glories       of his five predecessors to the ignominious fate of Nero and       Domitian.

Yet Commodus was not, as he has been represented, a tiger born       with an insatiate thirst of human blood, and capable, from his       infancy, of the most inhuman actions. 7 Nature had formed him of       a weak rather than a wicked disposition. His simplicity and       timidity rendered him the slave of his attendants, who gradually       corrupted his mind. His cruelty, which at first obeyed the       dictates of others, degenerated into habit, and at length became       the ruling passion of his soul. 8

Upon the death of his father, Commodus found himself embarrassed       with the command of a great army, and the conduct of a difficult       war against the Quadi and Marcomanni. 9 The servile and       profligate youths whom Marcus had banished, soon regained their       station and influence about the new emperor. They exaggerated the       hardships and dangers of a campaign in the wild countries beyond       the Danube; and they assured the indolent prince that the terror       of his name, and the arms of his lieutenants, would be sufficient       to complete the conquest of the dismayed barbarians, or to impose       such conditions as were more advantageous than any conquest. By a       dexterous application to his sensual appetites, they compared the       tranquillity, the splendor, the refined pleasures of Rome, with       the tumult of a Pannonian camp, which afforded neither leisure       nor materials for luxury. 10 Commodus listened to the pleasing       advice; but whilst he hesitated between his own inclination and       the awe which he still retained for his father’s counsellors, the       summer insensibly elapsed, and his triumphal entry into the       capital was deferred till the autumn. His graceful person, 11       popular address, and imagined virtues, attracted the public       favor; the honorable peace which he had recently granted to the       barbarians, diffused a universal joy; 12 his impatience to       revisit Rome was fondly ascribed to the love of his country; and       his dissolute course of amusements was faintly condemned in a       prince of nineteen years of age.

12 (return) [ This universal joy is well described (from the       medals as well as historians) by Mr. Wotton, Hist. of Rome, p.       192, 193.] During the three first years of his reign, the forms,       and even the spirit, of the old administration, were maintained       by those faithful counsellors, to whom Marcus had recommended his       son, and for whose wisdom and integrity Commodus still       entertained a reluctant esteem. The young prince and his       profligate favorites revelled in all the license of sovereign       power; but his hands were yet unstained with blood; and he had       even displayed a generosity of sentiment, which might perhaps       have ripened into solid virtue. 13 A fatal incident decided his       fluctuating character.

One evening, as the emperor was returning to the palace, through       a dark and narrow portico in the amphitheatre, 14 an assassin,       who waited his passage, rushed upon him with a drawn sword,       loudly exclaiming, “_The senate sends you this_.” The menace       prevented the deed; the assassin was seized by the guards, and       immediately revealed the authors of the conspiracy. It had been       formed, not in the state, but within the walls of the palace.       Lucilla, the emperor’s sister, and widow of Lucius Verus,       impatient of the second rank, and jealous of the reigning       empress, had armed the murderer against her brother’s life. She       had not ventured to communicate the black design to her second       husband, Claudius Pompeiarus, a senator of distinguished merit       and unshaken loyalty; but among the crowd of her lovers (for she       imitated the manners of Faustina) she found men of desperate       fortunes and wild ambition, who were prepared to serve her more       violent, as well as her tender passions. The conspirators       experienced the rigor of justice, and the abandoned princess was       punished, first with exile, and afterwards with death. 15

But the words of the assassin sunk deep into the mind of       Commodus, and left an indelible impression of fear and hatred       against the whole body of the senate. 151 Those whom he had       dreaded as importunate ministers, he now suspected as secret       enemies. The Delators, a race of men discouraged, and almost       extinguished, under the former reigns, again became formidable,       as soon as they discovered that the emperor was desirous of       finding disaffection and treason in the senate. That assembly,       whom Marcus had ever considered as the great council of the       nation, was composed of the most distinguished of the Romans; and       distinction of every kind soon became criminal. The possession of       wealth stimulated the diligence of the informers; rigid virtue       implied a tacit censure of the irregularities of Commodus;       important services implied a dangerous superiority of merit; and       the friendship of the father always insured the aversion of the       son. Suspicion was equivalent to proof; trial to condemnation.       The execution of a considerable senator was attended with the       death of all who might lament or revenge his fate; and when       Commodus had once tasted human blood, he became incapable of pity       or remorse.

Of these innocent victims of tyranny, none died more lamented       than the two brothers of the Quintilian family, Maximus and       Condianus; whose fraternal love has saved their names from       oblivion, and endeared their memory to posterity. Their studies       and their occupations, their pursuits and their pleasures, were       still the same. In the enjoyment of a great estate, they never       admitted the idea of a separate interest: some fragments are now       extant of a treatise which they composed in common; 152 and in       every action of life it was observed that their two bodies were       animated by one soul. The Antonines, who valued their virtues,       and delighted in their union, raised them, in the same year, to       the consulship; and Marcus afterwards intrusted to their joint       care the civil administration of Greece, and a great military       command, in which they obtained a signal victory over the       Germans. It has been calculated by       the ablest politicians, that no state, without being soon       exhausted, can maintain above the hundredth part of its members       in arms and idleness. But although this relative proportion may       be uniform, the influence of the army over the rest of the       society will vary according to the degree of its positive       strength. The advantages of military science and discipline       cannot be exerted, unless a proper number of soldiers are united       into one body, and actuated by one soul. With a handful of men,       such a union would be ineffectual; with an unwieldy host, it       would be impracticable; and the powers of the machine would be       alike destroyed by the extreme minuteness or the excessive weight       of its springs. To illustrate this observation, we need only       reflect, that there is no superiority of natural strength,       artificial weapons, or acquired skill, which could enable one man       to keep in constant subjection one hundred of his       fellow-creatures: the tyrant of a single town, or a small       district, would soon discover that a hundred armed followers were       a weak defence against ten thousand peasants or citizens; but a       hundred thousand well-disciplined soldiers will command, with       despotic sway, ten millions of subjects; and a body of ten or       fifteen thousand guards will strike terror into the most numerous       populace that ever crowded the streets of an immense capital.

The Prætorian bands, whose licentious fury was the first symptom       and cause of the decline of the Roman empire, scarcely amounted       to the last-mentioned number. 1 They derived their institution       from Augustus. That crafty tyrant, sensible that laws might       color, but that arms alone could maintain, his usurped dominion,       had gradually formed this powerful body of guards, in constant       readiness to protect his person, to awe the senate, and either to       prevent or to crush the first motions of rebellion. He       distinguished these favored troops by a double pay and superior       privileges; but, as their formidable aspect would at once have       alarmed and irritated the Roman people, three cohorts only were       stationed in the capital, whilst the remainder was dispersed in       the adjacent towns of Italy. 2 But after fifty years of peace and       servitude, Tiberius ventured on a decisive measure, which forever       rivetted the fetters of his country. Under the fair pretences of       relieving Italy from the heavy burden of military quarters, and       of introducing a stricter discipline among the guards, he       assembled them at Rome, in a permanent camp, 3 which was       fortified with skilful care, 4 and placed on a commanding       situation. 5

5 (return) [ Close to the walls of the city, on the broad summit       of the Quirinal and Viminal hills. See Nardini Roma Antica, p.       174. Donatus de Roma Antiqua, p. 46. * Note: Not on both these       hills: neither Donatus nor Nardini justify this position.       (Whitaker’s Review. p. 13.) At the northern extremity of this       hill (the Viminal) are some considerable remains of a walled       enclosure which bears all the appearance of a Roman camp, and       therefore is generally thought to correspond with the Castra       Prætoria. Cramer’s Italy 390.—M.]

Such formidable servants are always necessary, but often fatal to       the throne of despotism. By thus introducing the Prætorian guards       as it were into the palace and the senate, the emperors taught       them to perceive their own strength, and the weakness of the       civil government; to view the vices of their masters with       familiar contempt, and to lay aside that reverential awe, which       distance only, and mystery, can preserve towards an imaginary       power. In the luxurious idleness of an opulent city, their pride       was nourished by the sense of their irresistible weight; nor was       it possible to conceal from them, that the person of the       sovereign, the authority of the senate, the public treasure, and       the seat of empire, were all in their hands. To divert the       Prætorian bands from these dangerous reflections, the firmest and       best established princes were obliged to mix blandishments with       commands, rewards with punishments, to flatter their pride,       indulge their pleasures, connive at their irregularities, and to       purchase their precarious faith by a liberal donative; which,       since the elevation of Claudius, was enacted as a legal claim, on       the accession of every new emperor. 6

6 (return) [ Claudius, raised by the soldiers to the empire, was       the first who gave a donative. He gave quina dena, 120l. (Sueton.       in Claud. c. 10: ) when Marcus, with his colleague Lucius Versus,       took quiet possession of the throne, he gave vicena, 160l. to       each of the guards. Hist. August. p. 25, (Dion, l. lxxiii. p.       1231.) We may form some idea of the amount of these sums, by       Hadrian’s complaint that the promotion of a Cæsar had cost him       ter millies, two millions and a half sterling.]

The advocate of the guards endeavored to justify by arguments the       power which they asserted by arms; and to maintain that,       according to the purest principles of the constitution, _their_       consent was essentially necessary in the appointment of an       emperor. The election of consuls, of generals, and of       magistrates, however it had been recently usurped by the senate,       was the ancient and undoubted right of the Roman people. 7 But       where was the Roman people to be found? Not surely amongst the       mixed multitude of slaves and strangers that filled the streets       of Rome; a servile populace, as devoid of spirit as destitute of       property. The defenders of the state, selected from the flower of       the Italian youth, 8 and trained in the exercise of arms and       virtue, were the genuine representatives of the people, and the       best entitled to elect the military chief of the republic. These       assertions, however defective in reason, became unanswerable when       the fierce Prætorians increased their weight, by throwing, like       the barbarian conqueror of Rome, their swords into the scale. 9

The Prætorians had violated the sanctity of the throne by the       atrocious murder of Pertinax; they dishonored the majesty of it       by their subsequent conduct. The camp was without a leader, for       even the præfect Lætus, who had excited the tempest, prudently       declined the public indignation. Amidst the wild disorder,       Sulpicianus, the emperor’s father-in-law, and governor of the       city, who had been sent to the camp on the first alarm of mutiny,       was endeavoring to calm the fury of the multitude, when he was       silenced by the clamorous return of the murderers, bearing on a       lance the head of Pertinax. Though history has accustomed us to       observe every principle and every passion yielding to the       imperious dictates of ambition, it is scarcely credible that, in       these moments of horror, Sulpicianus should have aspired to       ascend a throne polluted with the recent blood of so near a       relation and so excellent a prince. He had already begun to use       the only effectual argument, and to treat for the Imperial       dignity; but the more prudent of the Prætorians, apprehensive       that, in this private contract, they should not obtain a just       price for so valuable a commodity, ran out upon the ramparts;       and, with a loud voice, proclaimed that the Roman world was to be       disposed of to the best bidder by public auction. 10

The passage is a compact, 19th‑century historiographical essay that makes a single, sweeping claim: *the Praetorian Guard was a powerful political force in the early Roman Empire, and the historical record confirms this.*  The author supports the claim with a mixture of quantitative reasoning, vivid historical anecdotes, and appeals to classical authority.  By analysing the argument, its rhetorical machinery and its place in the broader history of the Roman principate, we can see how the passage works, what its limits are, and why it remains a useful illustration of early‑imperial politics.

---

## 1. Main Argument in Brief

1. **Premise (general principle).**  
   The “power of the sword” is most effective in a large, centrally organised state; a small community cannot sustain a comparable military force without exhausting its resources.  (Lines 1‑13)

2. **Application to the Praetorian Guard.**  
   Because the Guard is a large, disciplined body united under one command, it can exert disproportionate influence over Roman society and the imperial throne.

3. **Historical evidence.**  
   * Augustus created the Guard as a permanent, double‑pay unit (footnote 1).  
   * Tiberius later concentrated the Guard in a permanent camp at the Quirinal/Viminal hills, giving it a permanent, militarised presence (footnotes 2‑5).  
   * Emperors repeatedly bought the Guard’s loyalty with donatives, a practice that began with Claudius and continued throughout the early principate (footnote 6).  
   * The Guard’s political potency is illustrated by the mutinies of AD 19‑23, the murder of Pertinax in AD 193, and the threat they posed to imperial authority (lines 30‑44).

4. **Conclusion.**  
   The Guard’s size, discipline and the emperors’ dependence on its support make it a decisive political actor; its very existence helped to undermine the stability of the imperial system.

---

## 2. Rhetorical Style and Structure

| Element | How it is Used | Effect |
|---------|----------------|--------|
| **Enumeration & Parallelism** | Lists of “three cohorts only,” “ten or fifteen thousand guards,” “the sword… in an extensive monarchy” (lines 1‑13, 30‑33). | Creates a rhythmic, memorable cadence that reinforces the quantitative claims. |
| **Analogy & Metaphor** | “Power of the sword… more sensibly felt in an extensive monarchy” (line 1); “the machine… destroyed by the extreme minuteness or the excessive weight of its springs” (line 17). | Translates abstract military concepts into mechanical images, suggesting a balance that must be achieved. |
| **Causal Chains** | “He assembled them… which forever rivetted the fetters of his country” (line 23); “the Guard’s pride was nourished… nor was it possible to conceal… that the person of the sovereign… were all in their hands.” | Links Tiberius’s re‑organisation directly to the entrenchment of despotism, presenting the Guard as the engine of political change. |
| **Appeal to Authority** | Frequent citations of Suetonius, Tacitus, the *Historia Augusta*, and modern scholars (footnotes 1‑6). | Lends scholarly gravitas; the footnote apparatus signals that the argument is built on both ancient testimony and contemporary scholarship. |
| **Hyperbole & Vivid Imagery** | “licentious fury,” “despotic sway,” “forever rivetted the fetters,” “strike terror into the most numerous populace.” | Heightens emotional impact, portraying the Guard not merely as a military unit but as a looming, almost mythic threat. |
| **Chronological Narrative** | A clear progression from Augustus’s foundation (c. 27 BC) → Tiberius’s concentration (c. AD 14) → Claudius’s donatives (AD 41) → Pertinax’s murder (AD 193). | Shows a causal line: institutional creation → structural entrenchment → political leverage → crisis. |
| **Implicit Moral Judgment** | The Guard is portrayed as “dangerous,” “prideful,” and “fatal to the throne of despotism.” | Signals the author’s view that the Guard’s political power is inherently destabilising, echoing republican critiques of imperial militarism. |

The passage is therefore **argumentatively tight**: a single claim is introduced, quantified, illustrated, and finally affirmed.  The rhetorical devices serve both to persuade the learned reader and to dramatise the political stakes of the Guard’s existence.

---

## 3. Historical Context

### 3.1. The Praetorian Guard in the Early Empire

| Date | Event | Relevance to the Passage |
|------|-------|--------------------------|
| **27 BC** (Augustus’s rise) | Augustus creates a **double‑pay, elite cohort** to protect his person and to counterbalance the Senate. | The passage cites this as the origin of the Guard’s “powerful body of guards” (footnote 1). |
| **c. AD 14** (Tiberius) | Concentrates the Guard in a permanent camp on the Quirinal/Viminal hills (the *Castra Praetoria*). | The footnotes describing the hill‑top camp (footnote 5) and the “permanent camp” (line 23) echo this development. |
| **AD 41** (Claudius) | Introduces **donatives** (large cash payments) to secure the Guard’s loyalty. | The passage’s discussion of “donatives” (lines 34‑38, footnote 6) reflects this practice. |
| **AD 19‑23** (mutinies) | The Guard repeatedly mutineers, demanding higher pay and political influence. | The narrative of “mutiny” and “terror” (lines 30‑38) draws directly on these crises. |
| **AD 193** (Pertinax) | The Guard murders the newly‑acclaimed emperor, demonstrating its capacity to decide imperial succession. | The murder of Pertinax (lines 44‑46) is the textbook illustration of the Guard’s political leverage. |

### 3.2. Why the Guard Was a Political Force

1. **Size and Cohesion** – A unit of 10–15 000 men, trained in *discipline* and *military science*, could act as a *single, unified will* (line 17).  Such cohesion is what the passage stresses as a prerequisite for any effective force.
2. **Economic Leverage** – Donatives turned the Guard from a purely military institution into a *client* of the emperor, but also made the emperor financially dependent on the Guard’s goodwill.
3. **Physical Presence** – Stationed in the capital, the Guard could intimidate the Senate, the populace, and rival claimants in ways no other institution could.
4. **Symbolic Authority** – By holding the *imperial standard* and the *person of the emperor* within their ranks, the Guard claimed a quasi‑sacred status that blurred the line between military service and political power.

### 3.3. The Wider Imperial Landscape

The passage reflects a **Republican‑leaning historiographical perspective** that sees the rise of the Praetorian Guard as a symptom of the erosion of traditional civic authority.  In the early principate, the emperor’s power was still *derived* from, and *checked* by, the army; the Guard was the most visible manifestation of that dependence.  By the mid‑2nd century, the Guard’s unchecked influence contributed to the “*prætorian*” crises that culminated in the Year of the Four Emperors (AD 69) and the eventual decline of the unit under Severus and later abolition by Constantine.

---

| **Quantitative Claim** | The “hundredth part” argument mirrors contemporary demographic reasoning (e.g., Machiavelli’s *Principe* on the size of standing armies). | The proportion is presented as a universal law; modern scholarship (e.g., Parker, *Polybius* on Roman manpower) suggests that political, not purely economic, factors were more decisive. |
| **Causality** | The link between Tiberius’s camp‑building and the Guard’s “forever‑rivetted fetters” is a clear causal chain. | The passage sometimes conflates *correlation* (e.g., donatives) with *causation* (e.g., the Guard’s “pride” causing imperial instability). |
| **Rhetorical Persuasion** | Vivid language makes the Guard’s threat palpable; enumeration aids memory. | The hyperbolic tone may overstate the Guard’s influence, risking a moralistic bias rather than a balanced assessment. |
| **Historiographical Context** | By invoking modern scholars (Nardini, Cramer, Whitaker), the author positions his work as part of a scholarly tradition. | The footnote apparatus is extensive but occasionally redundant; the argument could have benefitted from a brief synthesis of contemporary scholarship rather than a simple citation list. |

Overall, the passage **effectively illustrates** the political potency of the Praetorian Guard, but it does so with a **selective emphasis** on moments of crisis.  The strengths of its evidence lie in the breadth of primary attestations; the weaknesses lie in its tendency to present the Guard as an *inevitable* destabilising force rather than as one of several competing political actors.

---

## 5. Conclusion

The text’s main argument—*the Praetorian Guard was a powerful political force in the early Roman Empire*—is built on a tight logical structure, reinforced by vivid analogies, enumerations, and a chain of historical examples ranging from Augustus’s foundation to the murder of Pertinax.  Its rhetorical style, while florid, serves to dramatise the Guard’s capacity to shape imperial policy, to intimidate the Senate, and to extract financial favours from the emperor.  Historically, the Guard’s size, permanent presence in the capital, and the emperors’ dependence on donatives indeed gave it a unique, if not always decisive, political lever.  The passage thus offers a concise, though partially moralising, portrait of early‑imperial politics, one that remains a useful entry point for any study of the Roman army’s role in statecraft.

He was employed in a distant honorable command, when       he received a confidential letter from the emperor, acquainting       him of the treasonable designs of some discontented generals, and       authorizing him to declare himself the guardian and successor of       the throne, by assuming the title and ensigns of Cæsar. 18 The       governor of Britain wisely declined the dangerous honor, which       would have marked him for the jealousy, or involved him in the       approaching ruin, of Commodus. Personal merit alone had raised Pescennius Niger, from an obscure       birth and station, to the government of Syria; a lucrative and       important command, which in times of civil confusion gave him a       near prospect of the throne. His province extended to the Julian       Alps, which gave an easy access into Italy; and he remembered the       saying of Augustus, that a Pannonian army might in ten days       appear in sight of Rome. 31 By a celerity proportioned to the       greatness of the occasion, he might reasonably hope to revenge       Pertinax, punish Julian, and receive the homage of the senate and       people, as their lawful emperor, before his competitors,       separated from Italy by an immense tract of sea and land, were       apprised of his success, or even of his election. The wretched Julian had expected, and thought himself prepared,       to dispute the empire with the governor of Syria; but in the       invincible and rapid approach of the Pannonian legions, he saw       his inevitable ruin. The hasty arrival of every messenger       increased his just apprehensions. He was successively informed,       that Severus had passed the Alps; that the Italian cities,       unwilling or unable to oppose his progress, had received him with       the warmest professions of joy and duty; that the important place       of Ravenna had surrendered without resistance, and that the       Hadriatic fleet was in the hands of the conqueror. The enemy was       now within two hundred and fifty miles of Rome; and every moment       diminished the narrow span of life and empire allotted to Julian.

He attempted, however, to prevent, or at least to protract, his       ruin. He implored the venal faith of the Prætorians, filled the       city with unavailing preparations for war, drew lines round the       suburbs, and even strengthened the fortifications of the palace;       as if those last intrenchments could be defended, without hope of       relief, against a victorious invader. The unhappy discord of his sons       clouded all his prospects, and threatened to overturn a throne       raised with so much labor, cemented with so much blood, and       guarded with every defence of arms and treasure. With an       impartial hand he maintained between them an exact balance of       favor, conferred on both the rank of Augustus, with the revered       name of Antoninus; and for the first time the Roman world beheld       three emperors. 10 Yet even this equal conduct served only to       inflame the contest, whilst the fierce Caracalla asserted the       right of primogeniture, and the milder Geta courted the       affections of the people and the soldiers. In the anguish of a       disappointed father, Severus foretold that the weaker of his sons       would fall a sacrifice to the stronger; who, in his turn, would       be ruined by his own vices. 11

In these circumstances the intelligence of a war in Britain, and       of an invasion of the province by the barbarians of the North,       was received with pleasure by Severus. Though the vigilance of       his lieutenants might have been sufficient to repel the distant       enemy, he resolved to embrace the honorable pretext of       withdrawing his sons from the luxury of Rome, which enervated       their minds and irritated their passions; and of inuring their       youth to the toils of war and government. Notwithstanding his       advanced age, (for he was above threescore,) and his gout, which       obliged him to be carried in a litter, he transported himself in       person into that remote island, attended by his two sons, his       whole court, and a formidable army. He immediately passed the       walls of Hadrian and Antoninus, and entered the enemy’s country,       with a design of completing the long attempted conquest of       Britain. He penetrated to the northern extremity of the island,       without meeting an enemy. But the concealed ambuscades of the       Caledonians, who hung unseen on the rear and flanks of his army,       the coldness of the climate and the severity of a winter march       across the hills and morasses of Scotland, are reported to have       cost the Romans above fifty thousand men. The Caledonians at       length yielded to the powerful and obstinate attack, sued for       peace, and surrendered a part of their arms, and a large tract of       territory. But their apparent submission lasted no longer than       the present terror. As soon as the Roman legions had retired,       they resumed their hostile independence. Their restless spirit       provoked Severus to send a new army into Caledonia, with the most       bloody orders, not to subdue, but to extirpate the natives. They       were saved by the death of their haughty enemy. 12

This Caledonian war, neither marked by decisive events, nor       attended with any important consequences, would ill deserve our       attention; but it is supposed, not without a considerable degree       of probability, that the invasion of Severus is connected with       the most shining period of the British history or fable. ### 1. Main Argument  

The author argues that the decline of the Roman Empire in the 3rd century was the result of a confluence of political, military, and financial weaknesses that were especially evident in the reign of **Alexander Severus**. He makes this case in three inter‑related parts:

1. **Weak Leadership and Personal Failures** – Alexander’s “amiable” character and “inadequate abilities” were no match for the formidable challenges he faced. His mother, **Mamæa**, exercised an excessive, avaricious influence that tarnished his reputation and exposed him to ridicule. The “soft climate of Syria” is presented as a formative factor that cultivated a “tincture of weakness and effeminacy” in the prince.

2. **Military Discontent and the Persian Campaign** – The Persian war fatigued the army, and the disputed outcome of that campaign (defeat according to Herodian, but glorious victory according to other sources) amplified the troops’ discontent. The failure to secure a decisive victory, combined with the perception of Alexander as a poor general, eroded both his authority and the empire’s prestige.

3. **Structural and Fiscal Crises** – The “dangerous power of the army” grew under Commodus, the Severan dynasty’s “new maxims of policy,” and the “internal change” that undermined the faint image of law and liberty. The author also notes the significance of **Caracalla’s edict** granting citizenship to all free inhabitants, arguing that its “unbounded liberality” stemmed from avarice rather than genuine generosity, foreshadowing later fiscal strain.

Overall, the passage contends that **personal failings, military mutinies, and fiscal policies** together precipitated a cascade of internal calamities that ultimately contributed to the empire’s collapse.

**Main Argument**

The passage is a carefully staged piece of propaganda for the Senate’s decision, in the chaotic year 238 AD, to appoint the two men Maximus (originally the pre‑fect of Egypt) and Balbinus (a Roman aristocrat) as joint emperors.  Its thrust can be summarised in three inter‑locking claims:

1. **The empire is under an intolerable tyranny.**  The subjects of Maximin “are reduced to that uncommon distress… in which the body of the people has more to fear from oppression than from resistance.”  The narrative of the fall of Carthage at the hands of Capellius of Mauritania and the ignominious death of the Gordians dramatise the danger that a despotic ruler (Maximin) poses to liberty.

2. **The Senate alone can restore freedom and organise a defence.**  After the loss of the “two excellent princes” (the Gordians) the senate “cannot any longer practise cautious, dilatory measures.”  It therefore must either meet Maximin in battle or accept humiliating death.  The choice of two capable men, each assigned to a distinct sphere (war and peace), is portrayed as the only viable solution.

3. **The appointment of Maximus and Balbinus is both morally and politically justified.**  Their virtues (Balbinus’ eloquence, Maximus’ martial record) are invoked to assure the crowd that the Republic’s hopes are not extinguished.  The Senate’s appeal to “the merit of the candidates, universally acknowledged,” and the popular acclamations (“Long life and victory…”) present the new rulers as the legitimate heirs of the imperial office.

Thus the passage argues that the Senate’s decision—to elevate Maximus and Balbinus, and later to concede a nominal third emperor to satisfy the mob—was a necessary, rational, and patriotic act to rescue Italy and the empire from the oppression of Maximin and to honour the memory of the fallen Gordians.

---

**Rhetorical Style**

The text is steeped in the classicising diction of late‑antique historiography (the very footnote markers show its dependence on Cicero, Caesar and other “authorities”).  Its persuasive machinery can be broken down as follows:

| Rhetorical Element | How it is Used |
|--------------------|----------------|
| **Elevated diction & formulaic epithets** | “calm intrepidity,” “the cause of freedom,” “the most sanguine hopes,” “the rigid Maximus,” “the mild and humane Balbinus.”  The language lifts the debate from practical politics to a moral crusade. |
| **Antithesis** | “the choice of cautious, dilatory measures had been long since out of their power; that Maximin… was advancing… and that their only remaining alternative was either to meet him bravely… or tamely to expect the tortures…” (lines 27‑28) – juxtaposing delay vs. decisive action. |
| **Parallelism & Polysyndeton** | “to enrol and discipline the Italian youth; and instructed to fortify the ports and highways…” – the parallel infinitives create a rhythmic, marching effect, echoing a call‑to‑arms. |
| **Appeal to Authority (Ethos)** | Frequent citations of “Cicero,” “Caesar,” the “Supreme Pontiff,” and the “temple of Concord” bind the Senate’s decision to timeless Roman tradition.  The footnote references (e.g. 28) act as scholarly endorsements, reinforcing the text’s claim to historic legitimacy. |
| **Pathos – vivid imagery** | The gruesome picture of Carthage’s surrender, the “rapacious cruelty of a slave” demanding “blood and treasure,” the “uncommon distress” of Maximin’s subjects, all serve to evoke sympathy for the oppressed and revulsion at tyranny. |
| **Logos – logical progression** | The passage moves from a description of the crisis → the justification for Senate action → the virtues of the new emperors → the political impasse in Rome → a concession (the boy‑Caesar).  Each step supplies a logical reason for the next. |
| **Direct address** | “Ratify my choice, conscript fathers, or appoint in their place, others more worthy of the empire.”  This second‑person appeal is designed to mobilise the senatorial assembly itself. |
| **Climactic enumeration** | The final list of the two emperors’ qualifications (age, consular experience, military success, eloquence, pontifical office) builds a crescendo that frames them as the ideal joint leadership. |

Stylistically the passage mimics the *Historia Augusta*’s blend of “imperial biography” and “senatorial propaganda”: factual kernels (battle of the Gordians, Capellianus’ revolt) are wrapped in laudatory rhetoric that serves a political agenda rather than detached analysis.

---

**Historical Context**

The narrative reflects the tumultuous “Crisis of the Third Century” (c. 235‑284 AD), a period when the imperial office became a prize for ambitious generals and provincial rebels.  The specific events named correspond to the winter‑spring of 238 AD:

* **The death of Gordian III** (June 238) at the hands of Maximinus Thrax, whose heavy‑handed prefecture had turned him into a tyrant.  The “younger Gordian” sallies out with a handful of guards and is killed; his aged father, who had reigned only 36 days, follows him shortly thereafter.  

* **The revolt of Capellianus in Africa** – a governor of Mauritania who, with “a small band of veterans and a fierce host of barbarians,” captures Carthage, exposing the province to “the rapacious cruelty of a slave.”  This mirrors Herodian’s account of the African revolt that forced the imperial government to divert forces westward.

* **The joint accession of Maximus (originally the prefect of Egypt) and Balbinus (a Roman senator)** – a compromise solution endorsed by the Senate to divide the responsibilities of war (Maximus) and peace/administration (Balbinus).  The passage stresses their consular experience, age (60 / 74), and moral qualities, exactly the criteria ancient Roman politics demanded of “worthy” emperors.

* **The senatorial‑popular clash over a third emperor.**  The mob’s demand for a “boy‑Caesar” from the Gordian line reflects the deep‑seated desire for a symbolic restoration of the dynasty that had just been extinguished.  The concession (the appointment of a 13‑year‑old grandson) shows the Senate’s willingness to make a token gesture to preserve internal stability—a pattern seen in the later “puer‑emperor” phenomenon (e.g., Commodus, later Severan practice).

The text also alludes to the intertwining of secular and sacred authority: the Senate’s meeting in the “temple of Concord” and the conferring upon the emperors of the “Supreme Pontifical” office.  This mirrors the real‑world practice that imperial legitimacy was inseparable from religious endorsement, a point stressed by both pagan senators and later Christian writers.

In sum, the passage is a snapshot of early‑238 AD Roman political discourse: a crisis‑driven appeal to the Senate to act decisively, a rhetorical justification for a joint imperial duo, and a pragmatic manoeuvre to quell popular unrest by co‑opting traditionalist symbols (the boy‑Caesar, the pontifical office).  Its composition betrays the conventions of the *Historia Augusta*—a work that, while historically uneven, was crafted to furnish the imperial house with a gloss of legitimacy and moral superiority.

---

**Conclusion**

The excerpt is a masterful example of ancient Roman political propaganda: it advances a concrete policy (the appointment of Maximus and Balbinus) by weaving a tapestry of moral urgency, classical authority, and emotional appeal.  Its rhetorical arsenal—antitheses, parallel constructions, direct senatorial address, and vivid pathos—serves to convince both the elite and the masses that the Senate’s choice is not only pragmatic but also the salvation of the Republic.  Historically, the passage captures the febrile atmosphere of 238 AD, when the empire teetered between tyranny, provincial revolt, and the desperate search for a unifying, yet conventional, imperial image.  Through the lens of classical rhetoric, the text transforms a moment of chaos into a narrative of order, thereby echoing the very purpose of Roman historiography: to legitimize the power that wields authority in the name of liberty and tradition.

The death of a tyrant (traditionally Commodus) triggers a cascade of events that expose the Republic’s weakness:

* The army, out of necessity rather than choice, recognises Maximus and swears an oath to him.  
* Maximus attempts a moderate, reconciliatory address, but his gesture of a liberal donative and a solemn expiation cannot quell the Praetorians, who regard themselves as the true beneficiaries of any triumph.  
* The two co‑emperors, Maximus (the senator) and Balbinus (the general), are unable to cooperate; their silent rivalry prevents a united defence against the Praetorians.  
* When the Praetorians finally intervene, they strip, humiliate and put to death the co‑emperors, leaving the state without legitimate civil leadership.

The narrative of Gordian’s death (the “fortunate accident” that “delivered his confidence on a minister” ⁴⁸) and the Persian campaign (the army’s “regular plenty” and Misitheus’s disciplinary oversight ⁴⁹) shows the emperor’s dependence on military and court officials rather than on personal virtue or hereditary right. He engages **pathos** through moral condemnation (“pernicious vermin of the East” ⁴⁸) and lamentation for the “innocent prince” (¶ 2).  **Rhetorical questions** such as “We are ignorant by what fortunate accident…” (¶ 2) invite the reader’s reflection on the limits of historical knowledge.  The passage employs **analogy** (the Roman empire likened to the Algerian aristocracy and the Dey) and **antithesis** (“military government … more republican than monarchical”) to crystallise his argument. The passage is situated in the **mid‑third‑century crisis of the Roman Empire**.  Gordian III’s accession in 238, his death at only nineteen, and the regency of his mother (the “eunuchs” who “infested the Roman palace” since Elagabalus ⁴⁸) reflect the period’s increasing court intrigue and the erosion of civilian authority. Some ingenious writers 2 have suspected that Europe was much       colder formerly than it is at present; and the most ancient       descriptions of the climate of Germany tend exceedingly to       confirm their theory. The general complaints of intense frost and       eternal winter are perhaps little to be regarded, since we have       no method of reducing to the accurate standard of the       thermometer, the feelings, or the expressions, of an orator born       in the happier regions of Greece or Asia. But I shall select two       remarkable circumstances of a less equivocal nature. 1. The great       rivers which covered the Roman provinces, the Rhine and the       Danube, were frequently frozen over, and capable of supporting       the most enormous weights. The barbarians, who often chose that       severe season for their inroads, transported, without       apprehension or danger, their numerous armies, their cavalry, and       their heavy wagons, over a vast and solid bridge of ice. 3 Modern       ages have not presented an instance of a like phenomenon. 2. The       reindeer, that useful animal, from whom the savage of the North       derives the best comforts of his dreary life, is of a       constitution that supports, and even requires, the most intense       cold. Canada, at this day, is an exact picture of       ancient Germany. Although situated in the same parallel with the       finest provinces of France and England, that country experiences       the most rigorous cold. ### 1. Main Argument  

The author sets out to demonstrate that **ancient Germany was much colder than the climate of today**, and that this harsh climate left a distinct imprint on the land‑scape, the material culture, demography and physical character of the Germanic peoples.  His case rests on two “less equivocal” observations:

1. **Ice‑bound major rivers** – The Rhine and Danube were regularly frozen solid enough to support the weight of armies, heavy wagons and even the passage of whole legions on ice.  Such winter crossings, he notes, have never been recorded in modern times.  
2. **The presence and physiological specialisation of the reindeer** – The animal, adapted to extreme cold, is found far north (Spitzberg, Lapland, Siberia) and could not survive south of the Baltic in the present climate.  In Caesar’s day reindeer (and elk, wild bull) were native to the Hercynian forest, indicating a colder northern forest belt.

From these physical facts the author draws a chain of inferences:

* **Land‑scape change** – Modern deforestation, drainage of marshes and cultivation have warmed the air by allowing more solar radiation to reach the ground.  “Canada, at this day, is an exact picture of ancient Germany” – a colder, snow‑covered, river‑freed region.  
* **Human biology and society** – The “keen air” of ancient Germany is linked to taller, more robust, “masculine” bodies, higher fertility, bravery, and a propensity for violent exertion rather than patient labour.  The Romans’ winter campaigns were softened for the northern peoples, while the southern peoples suffered from summer heat.  
* **Historical demography** – The author suggests that the harsh climate favoured larger, more vigorous populations and that the “Indigenæ” of Tacitus reflect a native, indigenous stock that emerged from the Hercynian woods rather than from foreign colonies.

In short, climate is presented as a primary shaping force for ancient Germanic life, and the present milder climate is explained as the result of human‑induced environmental modification.

---

### 2. Rhetorical Style  

| Feature | How it is used in the passage |
|---------|--------------------------------|
| **Appeal to authority** | Frequent citations of classical writers (Diodorus Siculus, Herodian, Ovid, Virgil, Caesar, Tacitus, etc.) and modern scholars (the “M. 1845” footnotes). The author positions his argument within the scholarly tradition, lending it a veneer of objectivity. |
| **Use of “less equivocal” evidence** | By isolating two “clear” phenomena (ice‑bound rivers, reindeer), the author pre‑empts the objection that his reasoning is based on anecdote or speculation. |
| **Contrastive parallelism** | The two circumstances are presented in a numbered list, each described in a similar clause structure (“…were frequently frozen…”, “…is of a constitution…”) – a rhetorical device that emphasizes symmetry and balance. |
| **Inclusive “we” and “I”** | The writer adopts a collective scholarly stance (“we have no method of reducing…”, “I shall select”), inviting the reader to share the uncertainty while also asserting confidence in the conclusions drawn. |
| **Enumeration and cumulative force** | After the two primary points, the author adds a series of supporting observations (modern improvements, comparison with Canada, physiological effects) – a classic “argument by accumulation”. |
| **Concessions and caveats** | Acknowledges the lack of precise temperature measurement, the ambiguous classical descriptions of reindeer, and the difficulty of proving climate‑driven demographic trends. This softens potential criticism while preserving the main thrust. |
| **Scientific‑sounding language** | Words such as “supports, and even requires, the most intense cold”, “intercepted from the earth the rays of the sun”, “more temperate air” give the passage the veneer of a nascent environmental science. |

Overall, the style is that of a **19th‑century scholarly essay**: formal, densely footnoted, and deliberately cautious yet assertive, blending classical antiquarianism with emerging natural‑historical reasoning.

---

### 3. Historical Context  

1. **Intellectual milieu** – The passage reflects the **early‑to‑mid‑19th‑century German historical‑geographical tradition** (e.g., the work of scholars such as J. G. Herder, A. W. Erman, and later historians of the “Germanic” peoples).  At this time, classical sources were still mined for clues about ancient geography, climate and ethnography.  

2. **Climate‑determinism** – The idea that climate could shape national character and even the physical stature of a people was part of a broader **environmental‑determinist discourse** that linked geography, biology and history (cf. the works of Carl Ritter, Alexander von Humboldt).  The author’s argument fits neatly into this paradigm.  

3. **Romantic‑era view of “improvement”** – The claim that modern deforestation, drainage and cultivation have “warmed” the climate aligns with the **Enlightenment belief in human progress over nature**.  The notion that “Canada… is an exact picture of ancient Germany” illustrates a romantic nostalgia for a “primeval” harshness that modern agriculture has softened.  

4. **Use of footnotes as scholarly apparatus** – The extensive bracketed citations (e.g., Diodorus Siculus v. 340, Caesar vi. 23, Tacitus c. 3) are typical of **mid‑19th‑century scholarly practice**, where primary sources were presented alongside editorial commentary (“M. 1845”).  The footnotes also serve to **legitimize** the author’s speculative climate reconstruction by linking it to respected classical testimony.  

5. **Emergence of environmental history** – Though the concept of “climate change” as a long‑term phenomenon was not yet fully articulated, the text anticipates later **environmental‑historical** approaches by arguing that **human activity (deforestation, drainage)** can modify climate on a regional scale.  

6. **National‑cultural debates** – The discussion of “Indigenæ” versus foreign colonists, the “Germanic” versus “Latin” character, and the emphasis on a native “Hercynian” origin reflect the **growing German‑nationalist historiography** of the period, which sought to trace the roots of the Germanic peoples back to a cold, rugged north.  

---

### 4. Critical Assessment (brief)

* **Evidence base** – The two “clear” phenomena are indeed the strongest points, but much of the argument rests on **inferential leaps**: e.g., from river‑ice to a general colder climate, from reindeer physiology to the absence of such animals south of the Baltic today.  The lack of quantitative temperature data limits the precision of the reconstruction.  

* **Anachronistic assumptions** – The modern notion that “clearing woods intercepts solar rays” presupposes a linear cause‑and‑effect relationship between land‑use and climate that would not have been obvious to 19th‑century scholars; contemporary climate science would now require more nuanced modelling.  

* **Interpretive bias** – The author’s emphasis on the “hardy” nature of the ancient Germanic peoples may reflect a **cultural bias** favoring the notion of a “noble barbarism” rather than a balanced assessment of demographic and ecological factors.  

* **Methodology** – The reliance on classical literary sources for climatic data is now seen as **problematic**; many of the cited passages are poetic or rhetorical rather than scientific.  Modern paleoclimatic proxies (tree rings, ice cores, lake sediments) would provide far more reliable evidence.  

Overall, the passage is a **landmark example of early climate‑historical scholarship**, illustrating how classical antiquity, emerging natural science, and nationalist historiography were woven together to explain the past climate of ancient Germany.

---

### 5. Concise Summary  

- **Main claim:** Ancient Germany was considerably colder; this cold shaped its rivers (regular ice bridges), its fauna (cold‑adapted reindeer), its landscape (dense northern forests, snow‑covered terrain), and its people (taller, hardy, brave, high fertility).  
- **Rhetorical strategy:** Authority‑based citations, clear “two‑point” evidence, inclusive scholarly voice, concession to uncertainty, and accumulation of supporting observations.  
- **Historical backdrop:** 19th‑century German scholarship on Germanic origins, climate‑determinism, early environmental history, and the practice of footnoting classical texts to bolster argument.  

These elements together reveal a text that, for its time, convincingly (if not rigorously) links climate to culture, while also exposing the methodological limits of its era.

Strong beer, a liquor extracted with very little art from wheat       or barley, and _corrupted_ (as it is strongly expressed by       Tacitus) into a certain semblance of wine, was sufficient for the       gross purposes of German debauchery. The Tuscan who betrayed his country to the Celtic       nations, attracted them into Italy by the prospect of the rich       fruits and delicious wines, the productions of a happier climate.       34 And in the same manner the German auxiliaries, invited into       France during the civil wars of the sixteenth century, were       allured by the promise of plenteous quarters in the provinces of       Champaigne and Burgundy. 35 Drunkenness, the most illiberal, but       not the most dangerous of _our_ vices, was sometimes capable, in       a less civilized state of mankind, of occasioning a battle, a       war, or a revolution.

The climate of ancient Germany has been modified, and the soil       fertilized, by the labor of ten centuries from the time of       Charlemagne. The same extent of ground which at present       maintains, in ease and plenty, a million of husbandmen and       artificers, was unable to supply a hundred thousand lazy warriors       with the simple necessaries of life. 36 The Germans abandoned       their immense forests to the exercise of hunting, employed in       pasturage the most considerable part of their lands, bestowed on       the small remainder a rude and careless cultivation, and then       accused the scantiness and sterility of a country that refused to       maintain the multitude of its inhabitants. When the return of       famine severely admonished them of the importance of the arts,       the national distress was sometimes alleviated by the emigration       of a third, perhaps, or a fourth part of their youth. 37 The       possession and the enjoyment of property are the pledges which       bind a civilized people to an improved country. But the Germans,       who carried with them what they most valued, their arms, their       cattle, and their women, cheerfully abandoned the vast silence of       their woods for the unbounded hopes of plunder and conquest. The       innumerable swarms that issued, or seemed to issue, from the       great storehouse of nations, were multiplied by the fears of the       vanquished, and by the credulity of succeeding ages. A warlike nation like the Germans, without either cities,       letters, arts, or money, found some compensation for this savage       state in the enjoyment of liberty. ### 1. Main Argument  

The passage argues that the ancient Germanic peoples were a **war‑like, poverty‑stricken, liberty‑loving nation** whose social and political organization was fundamentally different from that of the Mediterranean world.  Key points of the argument are:

1. **Economic and Cultural Traits** – Germanic tribes extracted “strong beer” with little art from wheat or barley, a “corrupted” product that, according to Tacitus, suited “German debauchery.”  They were not interested in commerce, agriculture, or the “advantageous” trade that the Romans pursued; instead they sought plunder and the “delicious wines” of Italy and Gaul.  

2. **Motivation for Expansion** – Their “intemperate thirst” for strong liquors and for richer wines spurred invasions of Roman‑controlled provinces.  The desire for foreign wine and the promise of plunder were cited as primary incentives for Germanic migrations and auxiliary service (e.g., during the sixteenth‑century civil wars in France).  

3. **Political Structure** – The Germans possessed **no cities, letters, arts, or money**, and therefore compensated for this “savage” condition by enjoying **liberty**.  Their political system was a **voluntary association for mutual defence**, expressed through tribal councils, assemblies of warriors, and the investiture of each free youth with a shield and spear.  Decision‑making rested with the assembly; magistrates could persuade but the people resolved and executed.  

4. **Liberty as a Social Glue** – Poverty “secured their freedom,” because “our desires and our possessions are the strongest fetters of despotism.”  Thus liberty functioned as a “compensation” for material want.  

5. **Population Myth** – The passage refutes the ancient claim (derived from Tacitus and perpetuated by later writers) that the Germanic peoples were *far more numerous* than modern inhabitants.  It aligns the names of “Mariana” and “Machiavelli” (who argued for the efficacy of force) against those of “Robertson” and “Hume” (who, in the author’s view, provide a more rational explanation).  

6. **Exceptions and Regional Variations** – While most Germanic tribes were democratic, some coastal groups (the Suiones, Sitones) accepted kingship without relinquishing personal rights, illustrating that “the great historian sufficiently acknowledges the general theory of government.”  

In sum, the author presents the Germanic past as a **poverty‑driven, liberty‑oriented, militaristic society** whose institutions and motivations differ sharply from those of the Roman world, and he uses contemporary historiography to undermine exaggerated claims of ancient German over‑population.

The distinctions of the ferocious invaders were       perpetually varied by themselves, and confounded by the       astonished subjects of the Roman empire. 86

Wars, and the administration of public affairs, are the principal       subjects of history; but the number of persons interested in       these busy scenes is very different, according to the different       condition of mankind. In great monarchies, millions of obedient       subjects pursue their useful occupations in peace and obscurity. **Main argument (summary)**  
The author argues that the removal of the dissolute emperor Gallienus was the necessary prelude to a new era of “heroes” – most notably the soldier‑emperor Claudius II.  Gallienus is presented as a tyrant whose personal vices (luxury, lack of honour, indolence) brought calamity on Rome, and his death creates the political space for a competent, militarily‑effective ruler.  The text moves from a broad moral condemnation of Gallienus, through the political machinations of the usurper Aureolus, to the diplomatic and military skill of Claudius, and finally to the formal ratification of Claudius’s accession by the Senate.  In short: *good government follows the removal of a corrupt ruler; the Senate and the army confirm the new, virtuous sovereign.*

---

### Rhetorical style  

| Feature | How it is used in the passage | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Moralising tone** | Repeated denunciations of Gallienus as “destitute of a sense of honour”, “indolent”, “dissolute”. | Creates a clear moral hierarchy: tyrant → hero. |
| **Vivid battle imagery** | “the walls were battered with every engine … the bridge of Pontirolo … a mortal dart … nocturnal tumult”. | Engages the reader, stresses the drama of the conflict. |
| **Enumeration & parallelism** | Lists of Gallienus’s faults; list of conspirators (Heraclianus, Marcian, Cecrops). | Emphasises the breadth of corruption and the organized nature of the plot. |
| **Direct speeches (letters)** | The epistolary exchange (letter #4) gives voice to Claudius’s cunning. | Allows the author to reveal character through “saying” rather than only “doing”. |
| **Classical allusion** | References to ancient siege‑engine practices, the “imperial purple”, “the consulship”. | Positions the events within the tradition of Roman grandeur and legitimacy. |
| **Antithesis** | “the indignation of the people imputed all their calamities to Gallienus … the far greater part were, indeed, the consequence of his dissolute manners”. | Highlights the gap between popular blame and underlying cause. |
| **Hyperbole** | “the walls were battered with every engine … the siege … seldom disturbed the tranquil course of his pleasures”. | Underscores the author’s dramatic stance and the perceived invincibility of Gallienus while he is alive. |
| **Implicit persuasive appeal** | The author repeatedly urges the reader to “remember” Gallienus’s downfall (“We must not forget the lament…”). | Reinforces the moral lesson and seeks to legitise the new regime. |

Overall, the passage blends historiographical narrative with rhetorical flourish, turning events into moral exemplars.

---

### Historical context  

*Time‑frame*: The events belong to the middle‑3rd‑century “Crisis” (c. 268‑275 CE). Gallienus (emperor 268‑275) ruled a fractured empire plagued by internal usurpations, barbarian pressure on the Danube frontier, and fiscal exhaustion.  

*Key figures*  
- **Gallienus** – a court‑focused emperor whose luxury made him vulnerable to conspirators.  
- **Aureolus** – a Raetian usurper who raised an army on the Upper Danube, invaded Italy, and threatened Rome.  
- **Claudius II (Claudius Gothicus)** – a senior Illyrian commander who, after Gallienus’s assassination, is proclaimed emperor and quickly restores order.  

*Political institutions* – The Senate is portrayed as the traditional authority that validates a new ruler (ratifies Claudius, dispenses justice). Its role reflects the late‑antique tendency to appeal to “republican” legitimacy even as imperial power became increasingly militarised.  

*Military dynamics* – The text stresses donatives (20 gold pieces per soldier), the importance of legions in deciding succession, and the shift from “indolent” imperial rule to “active” command on the frontier (Thrace, Dacia, Pannonia, etc.).  

*Why the passage matters* – By casting Gallienus as a moral failure and Claudius as a capable soldier‑emperor, the author participates in the 4th‑century historiographical debate over “good” versus “bad” Roman rule, using the past as a warning for contemporary leaders.

## Direct answers to the numbered questions  

1. **Author’s view of Emperor Gallienus**  
   The author depicts Gallienus as a *dissolute tyrant* lacking honour, whose “luxury” and “careless administration” bring disaster on the empire.  He is blamed for the calamities befalling Rome and is portrayed as unfit to rule; his removal is portrayed as a necessary pre‑condition for the arrival of true heroes.

2. **How the author describes Aureolus’s “effort”**  
   Aureolus is shown as an active usurper who employs *political intrigue* (forming conspiracies with Heraclianus, Marcian, Cecrops), *bribery and propaganda* (spreading libels, promising rewards), and *military negotiation* (seeking a treaty with Claudius).  His effort is therefore both *subversive* (plotting Gallienus’s murder) and *diplomatic* (trying to buy the loyalty of the troops and to secure foreign support).

3. **What the letter of Claudius to Gallienus (letter #4) illustrates about his character**  
   The letter reveals Claudius as a *cunning diplomat*: he acknowledges Gallienus’s grievances, offers lavish gifts (money, a wardrobe, silver‑gold service), and pleads for reconciliation while warning that the Illyrian troops are already “provoked”.  He uses flattery (“I have sent him some presents…”) and strategic secrecy (“let it not reach the knowledge of the Dacian troops”).  This shows a ruler who values *political survival* over personal enmity and who is comfortable mixing *generosity with manipulation*.

4. **Outcome of the siege of Milan**  
   After Gallienus’s assassination, Aureolus’s siege continues but fails.  Faced with a united Roman front, Aureolus is forced to **surrender the city and himself**, is **executed** (the Senate’s judgment), and Claudius is formally **ratified as emperor**.  The siege thus ends in the triumph of the lawful (Claudian) authority.

5. **Author’s attitude toward the Senate**  
   The author largely **supports the Senate’s role** in legitimising Claudius, ratifying his election, and dispensing “justice” against usurpers.  He also hints that the Senate’s zeal can be harsh (“severe revenge against his friends and family”), but overall the Senate is presented as a stabilising, traditional authority that upholds the proper order of the Republic‑imperial system.

6. **“We must not forget the lament…”**  
   This injunction functions as a **moral warning**: the narrator urges future readers (or rulers) to remember the *lament* over Gallienus’s downfall, i.e., to keep in mind his vices and the lessons his removal taught about the dangers of luxury, indecision, and lack of honour.  It reinforces the author’s broader argument that a ruler’s moral character determines the fate of the empire.

### Concise synthesis  

- **Main claim**: The empire is saved by replacing a corrupt, effeminate emperor (Gallienus) with a capable, soldier‑emperor (Claudius), and the Senate’s ratification seals the new order.  
- **Rhetoric**: Moral condemnation, vivid battlefield description, enumerated faults, direct epistolary evidence, and classical allusion work together to turn history into a didactic lesson.  
- **Context**: The passage reflects 4th‑century historiography’s fascination with the 3rd‑century “Crisis”; it uses the episode to illustrate the perils of decadent rulership and the restorative power of military virtue, while also showcasing the continuing constitutional role of the Senate.  

Thus the text serves both as a **chronicle of events** and as a **moral‑political tract** aimed at reminding contemporaries (or later readers) why a ruler like Gallienus must be shunned and why a man like Claudius is fit to wear the purple.
