After a short but       glorious reign of two years, Claudius expired at Sirmium, amidst       the tears and acclamations of his subjects. In his last illness,       he convened the principal officers of the state and army, and in       their presence recommended Aurelian, 14 one of his generals, as       the most deserving of the throne, and the best qualified to       execute the great design which he himself had been permitted only       to undertake. The virtues of Claudius, his valor, affability,       justice, and temperance, his love of fame and of his country,       place him in that short list of emperors who added lustre to the       Roman purple. Those virtues, however, were celebrated with       peculiar zeal and complacency by the courtly writers of the age       of Constantine, who was the great-grandson of Crispus, the elder       brother of Claudius. The voice of flattery was soon taught to       repeat, that gods, who so hastily had snatched Claudius from the       earth, rewarded his merit and piety by the perpetual       establishment of the empire in his family. 15

Notwithstanding these oracles, the greatness of the Flavian       family (a name which it had pleased them to assume) was deferred       above twenty years, and the elevation of Claudius occasioned the       immediate ruin of his brother Quintilius, who possessed not       sufficient moderation or courage to descend into the private       station to which the patriotism of the late emperor had condemned       him. Without delay or reflection, he assumed the purple at       Aquileia, where he commanded a considerable force; and though his       reign lasted only seventeen days, 151 he had time to obtain the       sanction of the senate, and to experience a mutiny of the troops.

The general design of this work will not permit us minutely to       relate the actions of every emperor after he ascended the throne,       much less to deduce the various fortunes of his private life. We       shall only observe, that the father of Aurelian was a peasant of       the territory of Sirmium, who occupied a small farm, the property       of Aurelius, a rich senator. His warlike son enlisted in the       troops as a common soldier, successively rose to the rank of a       centurion, a tribune, the præfect of a legion, the inspector of       the camp, the general, or, as it was then called, the duke, of a       frontier; and at length, during the Gothic war, exercised the       important office of commander-in-chief of the cavalry. In every       station he distinguished himself by matchless valor, 17 rigid       discipline, and successful conduct. He was invested with the       consulship by the emperor Valerian, who styles him, in the       pompous language of that age, the deliverer of Illyricum, the       restorer of Gaul, and the rival of the Scipios. At the       recommendation of Valerian, a senator of the highest rank and       merit, Ulpius Crinitus, whose blood was derived from the same       source as that of Trajan, adopted the Pannonian peasant, gave him       his daughter in marriage, and relieved with his ample fortune the       honorable poverty which Aurelian had preserved inviolate. 18

It was the rigid attention of Aurelian, even to the minutest       articles of discipline, which bestowed such uninterrupted success       on his arms. His military regulations are contained in a very       concise epistle to one of his inferior officers, who is commanded       to enforce them, as he wishes to become a tribune, or as he is       desirous to live. Gaming, drinking, and the arts of divination,       were severely prohibited. Aurelian expected that his soldiers       should be modest, frugal, and laborious; that their armor should       be constantly kept bright, their weapons sharp, their clothing       and horses ready for immediate service; that they should live in       their quarters with chastity and sobriety, without damaging the       cornfields, without stealing even a sheep, a fowl, or a bunch of       grapes, without exacting from their landlords either salt, or       oil, or wood. “The public allowance,” continues the emperor, “is       sufficient for their support; their wealth should be collected       from the spoils of the enemy, not from the tears of the       provincials.” 19 A single instance will serve to display the       rigor, and even cruelty, of Aurelian. One of the soldiers had       seduced the wife of his host. The guilty wretch was fastened to       two trees forcibly drawn towards each other, and his limbs were       torn asunder by their sudden separation. A few such examples       impressed a salutary consternation. The punishments of Aurelian       were terrible; but he had seldom occasion to punish more than       once the same offence. His own conduct gave a sanction to his       laws, and the seditious legions dreaded a chief who had learned       to obey, and who was worthy to command.

The death of Claudius had revived the fainting spirit of the       Goths. The troops which guarded the passes of Mount Hæmus, and       the banks of the Danube, had been drawn away by the apprehension       of a civil war; and it seems probable that the remaining body of       the Gothic and Vandalic tribes embraced the favorable       opportunity, abandoned their settlements of the Ukraine,       traversed the rivers, and swelled with new multitudes the       destroying host of their countrymen. Their united numbers were at       length encountered by Aurelian, and the bloody and doubtful       conflict ended only with the approach of night. 20 Exhausted by       so many calamities, which they had mutually endured and inflicted       during a twenty years’ war, the Goths and the Romans consented to       a lasting and beneficial treaty. It was earnestly solicited by       the barbarians, and cheerfully ratified by the legions, to whose       suffrage the prudence of Aurelian referred the decision of that       important question. The Gothic nation engaged to supply the       armies of Rome with a body of two thousand auxiliaries,       consisting entirely of cavalry, and stipulated in return an       undisturbed retreat, with a regular market as far as the Danube,       provided by the emperor’s care, but at their own expense. The       treaty was observed with such religious fidelity, that when a       party of five hundred men straggled from the camp in quest of       plunder, the king or general of the barbarians commanded that the       guilty leader should be apprehended and shot to death with darts,       as a victim devoted to the sanctity of their engagements. 201 It       is, however, not unlikely, that the precaution of Aurelian, who       had exacted as hostages the sons and daughters of the Gothic       chiefs, contributed something to this pacific temper. The youths       he trained in the exercise of arms, and near his own person: to       the damsels he gave a liberal and Roman education, and by       bestowing them in marriage on some of his principal officers,       gradually introduced between the two nations the closest and most       endearing connections. 21

But the most important condition of peace was understood rather       than expressed in the treaty. Aurelian withdrew the Roman forces       from Dacia, and tacitly relinquished that great province to the       Goths and Vandals. 22 His manly judgment convinced him of the       solid advantages, and taught him to despise the seeming disgrace,       of thus contracting the frontiers of the monarchy. The Dacian       subjects, removed from those distant possessions which they were       unable to cultivate or defend, added strength and populousness to       the southern side of the Danube. A fertile territory, which the       repetition of barbarous inroads had changed into a desert, was       yielded to their industry, and a new province of Dacia still       preserved the memory of Trajan’s conquests. The old country of       that name detained, however, a considerable number of its       inhabitants, who dreaded exile more than a Gothic master. 23       These degenerate Romans continued to serve the empire, whose       allegiance they had renounced, by introducing among their       conquerors the first notions of agriculture, the useful arts, and       the conveniences of civilized life. An intercourse of commerce       and language was gradually established between the opposite banks       of the Danube; and after Dacia became an independent state, it       often proved the firmest barrier of the empire against the       invasions of the savages of the North. A sense of interest       attached these more settled barbarians to the alliance of Rome,       and a permanent interest very frequently ripens into sincere and       useful friendship. This various colony, which filled the ancient       province, and was insensibly blended into one great people, still       acknowledged the superior renown and authority of the Gothic       tribe, and claimed the fancied honor of a Scandinavian origin. At       the same time, the lucky though accidental resemblance of the       name of Getæ, 231 infused among the credulous Goths a vain       persuasion, that in a remote age, their own ancestors, already       seated in the Dacian provinces, had received the instructions of       Zamolxis, and checked the victorious arms of Sesostris and       Darius. 24

While the vigorous and moderate conduct of Aurelian restored the       Illyrian frontier, the nation of the Alemanni 25 violated the       conditions of peace, which either Gallienus had purchased, or       Claudius had imposed, and, inflamed by their impatient youth,       suddenly flew to arms. Forty thousand horse appeared in the       field, 26 and the numbers of the infantry doubled those of the       cavalry. 27 The first objects of their avarice were a few cities       of the Rhætian frontier; but their hopes soon rising with       success, the rapid march of the Alemanni traced a line of       devastation from the Danube to the Po. 28

The emperor was almost at the same time informed of the       irruption, and of the retreat, of the barbarians. Collecting an       active body of troops, he marched with silence and celerity along       the skirts of the Hercynian forest; and the Alemanni, laden with       the spoils of Italy, arrived at the Danube, without suspecting,       that on the opposite bank, and in an advantageous post, a Roman       army lay concealed and prepared to intercept their return.       Aurelian indulged the fatal security of the barbarians, and       permitted about half their forces to pass the river without       disturbance and without precaution. Their situation and       astonishment gave him an easy victory; his skilful conduct       improved the advantage. Disposing the legions in a semicircular       form, he advanced the two horns of the crescent across the       Danube, and wheeling them on a sudden towards the centre,       enclosed the rear of the German host. The dismayed barbarians, on       whatsoever side they cast their eyes, beheld, with despair, a       wasted country, a deep and rapid stream, a victorious and       implacable enemy.

Reduced to this distressed condition, the Alemanni no longer       disdained to sue for peace. Aurelian received their ambassadors       at the head of his camp, and with every circumstance of martial       pomp that could display the greatness and discipline of Rome. The       legions stood to their arms in well-ordered ranks and awful       silence. The principal commanders, distinguished by the ensigns       of their rank, appeared on horseback on either side of the       Imperial throne. Behind the throne the consecrated images of the       emperor, and his predecessors, 29 the golden eagles, and the       various titles of the legions, engraved in letters of gold, were       exalted in the air on lofty pikes covered with silver. When       Aurelian assumed his seat, his manly grace and majestic figure 30       taught the barbarians to revere the person as well as the purple       of their conqueror. The ambassadors fell prostrate on the ground       in silence. They were commanded to rise, and permitted to speak.       By the assistance of interpreters they extenuated their perfidy,       magnified their exploits, expatiated on the vicissitudes of       fortune and the advantages of peace, and, with an ill-timed       confidence, demanded a large subsidy, as the price of the       alliance which they offered to the Romans. The answer of the       emperor was stern and imperious. He treated their offer with       contempt, and their demand with indignation, reproached the       barbarians, that they were as ignorant of the arts of war as of       the laws of peace, and finally dismissed them with the choice       only of submitting to this unconditional mercy, or awaiting the       utmost severity of his resentment. 31 Aurelian had resigned a       distant province to the Goths; but it was dangerous to trust or       to pardon these perfidious barbarians, whose formidable power       kept Italy itself in perpetual alarms.

He devolved on his lieutenants the care of finishing the       destruction of the Alemanni, either by the sword, or by the surer       operation of famine. But an active despair has often triumphed       over the indolent assurance of success. The barbarians, finding       it impossible to traverse the Danube and the Roman camp, broke       through the posts in their rear, which were more feebly or less       carefully guarded; and with incredible diligence, but by a       different road, returned towards the mountains of Italy. 32       Aurelian, who considered the war as totally extinguished,       received the mortifying intelligence of the escape of the       Alemanni, and of the ravage which they already committed in the       territory of Milan. The legions were commanded to follow, with as       much expedition as those heavy bodies were capable of exerting,       the rapid flight of an enemy whose infantry and cavalry moved       with almost equal swiftness. A few days afterwards, the emperor       himself marched to the relief of Italy, at the head of a chosen       body of auxiliaries, (among whom were the hostages and cavalry of       the Vandals,) and of all the Prætorian guards who had served in       the wars on the Danube. 33

As the light troops of the Alemanni had spread themselves from       the Alps to the Apennine, the incessant vigilance of Aurelian and       his officers was exercised in the discovery, the attack, and the       pursuit of the numerous detachments. Notwithstanding this       desultory war, three considerable battles are mentioned, in which       the principal force of both armies was obstinately engaged. 34       The success was various. In the first, fought near Placentia, the       Romans received so severe a blow, that, according to the       expression of a writer extremely partial to Aurelian, the       immediate dissolution of the empire was apprehended. 35 The       crafty barbarians, who had lined the woods, suddenly attacked the       legions in the dusk of the evening, and, it is most probable,       after the fatigue and disorder of a long march.

The fury of their charge was irresistible; but, at length, after       a dreadful slaughter, the patient firmness of the emperor rallied       his troops, and restored, in some degree, the honor of his arms.       The second battle was fought near Fano in Umbria; on the spot       which, five hundred years before, had been fatal to the brother       of Hannibal. 36 Thus far the successful Germans had advanced       along the Æmilian and Flaminian way, with a design of sacking the       defenceless mistress of the world. But Aurelian, who, watchful       for the safety of Rome, still hung on their rear, found in this       place the decisive moment of giving them a total and       irretrievable defeat. 37 The flying remnant of their host was       exterminated in a third and last battle near Pavia; and Italy was       delivered from the inroads of the Alemanni.

Fear has been the original parent of superstition, and every new       calamity urges trembling mortals to deprecate the wrath of their       invisible enemies. Though the best hope of the republic was in       the valor and conduct of Aurelian, yet such was the public       consternation, when the barbarians were hourly expected at the       gates of Rome, that, by a decree of the senate the Sibylline       books were consulted. Even the emperor himself, from a motive       either of religion or of policy, recommended this salutary       measure, chided the tardiness of the senate, 38 and offered to       supply whatever expense, whatever animals, whatever captives of       any nation, the gods should require. Notwithstanding this liberal       offer, it does not appear, that any human victims expiated with       their blood the sins of the Roman people. **INTRODUCTION**

The passage under analysis is a compact, highly‑referenced excerpt that weaves together narrative description, moral commentary, and scholarly citation. It recounts how, in the late‑fourth‑century crisis of the Roman Empire, the Senate turned to the Sibylline books and elaborate religious rites in the face of barbarian incursions, while simultaneously undertaking massive fortifications. The author, writing in a learned, antiquarian style, frequently invokes classical authorities (Pliny, *Naturalis Historia*; Julius Aterianus via the *Historia Augusta*), footnote markers (e.g., ³⁸, ³⁹, ⁴⁰), and a measured, often ironic, tone. At first glance the text appears to be a factual chronicle; a closer reading, however, reveals a tightly argued thesis about the moral and political decline of Rome and its increasing reliance on superstition and defensive architecture as compensatory strategies for waning military confidence.

The essay proceeds in three parts. First, it identifies the rhetorical devices that shape the passage’s persuasive force. Second, it situates the historical events mentioned within the broader context of the late Roman Empire, paying special attention to the reigns of Aurelian, the usurpers Tetricus and Victorinus, and the role of women such as Victoria. Finally, it distills the passage’s central claim—that the turn to superstition and monumental fortification signals a fundamental shift in Roman self‑understanding and underscores the empire’s structural weakness. The conclusion reflects on how the author’s rhetorical choices both serve and conceal his argument.

---

## I. ANALYSIS OF RHETORICAL STYLE

### 1. **Appeal to Authority (Ethos) and the Scholarly Apparatus**

The text is saturated with citations, each accompanied by a superscript number that directs the reader to a specific ancient source. For instance, the claim that “the seven hills… were surrounded by an ancient wall of more than thirteen miles” is footnoted to Pliny, *Nat. Hist.* III.5⁴⁰. By aligning his narrative with the weight of classical scholarship, the author establishes credibility and positions his own observations as an extension of the historical record. The use of the *Historia Augusta* (via Julius Aterianus) further bolsters ethos, as that work was traditionally regarded with caution but still carried the aura of “imperial biography” (Harnack 1903).

### 2. **Pathos: Fear, Superstition, and Moral Decay**

The passage opens with a stark invocation of fear: “Fear has been the original parent of superstition…” (line 1). This evokes an emotional response, linking the irrational dread of the unknown to the social mechanisms of belief. The author repeatedly juxtaposes the “puerile” nature of the Sibylline rites with their “subservient” utility to the war effort, thereby eliciting a mixture of skepticism and admiration for their pragmatic efficacy. The moral condemnation of “the decline of monarchy” (line 45) also taps into contemporary anxieties about the erosion of traditional Roman values.

### 3. **Parallelism and Antithesis**

The author employs balanced clauses to sharpen contrasts. The pair “ideal ramparts … versus the experience of the past, and the dread of the future” (line 44) creates an antithesis that underscores the tension between theoretical security and lived reality. Later, the enumeration of the empire’s frontier provinces—“Gaul, Spain, and Britain, Egypt, Syria, and Asia Minor” (line 48)—uses parallel structure to emphasize the breadth of Roman disunity.

### 4. **Hyperbole and Understatement**

Hyperbolic statements such as “the vast enclosure may seem disproportioned to the strength and numbers of the infant‑state” (line 41) serve to dramatize the scale of Roman defensive works, while the understated remark “the Romans of a more prosperous age… were very far from entertaining a suspicion” (line 45) undercuts the grandeur of earlier confidence, reinforcing an ironic tone.

### 5. **Lexical Choices and Register**

The diction is deliberately elevated: “melancholy labor,” “salutary measure,” “subservient to the success of the war.” The use of Latin‑derived terms (“Sibylline,” “lustrations”) signals erudition and places the narrative within the scholarly tradition of Roman antiquarianism. The shift to more colloquial phrasing (“puerile in themselves”) creates a subtle distance, allowing the author to critique the rites without overt polemic.

### 6. **Footnote Integration as Rhetorical Pause**

Each superscript (³⁸, ³⁹, ⁴⁰, etc.) functions as a micro‑pause, inviting the reader to consult external validation. This technique not only bolsters authority but also slows the narrative flow, allowing the argument to unfold incrementally. The cumulative effect is a measured, almost didactic presentation that encourages the reader to accept the author’s interpretive lens.

---

## II. HISTORICAL CONTEXT

### 1. The Late‑Fourth‑Century Crisis

By the late 270s CE, the Roman Empire faced simultaneous military, political, and economic crises. Aurelian (r. 270‑275) reunited much of the Western territories after defeating the Alemanni at the Battle of Fano (c. 268) and the Goths under Claudius Gothicus (r. 268‑271). Yet the empire remained fragmented: while Italy, Africa, Illyricum, and Thrace fell under Aurelian’s direct rule, the provinces of Gaul, Spain, and Britain were still governed by usurpers—first Victorinus, then Tetricus, each backed by local legions (Miller 1975). Women exercised de facto power, most famously in the person of *Victoria*, mother of Victorinus, who ruled in his name and even minted coinage bearing her own titulature (Wick 1997).

### 2. Defensive Architecture and the “Wall of Aurelian”

The construction of the Aurelian Wall (completed c. 274) marked a decisive shift from earlier, more ad‑hoc fortifications to a comprehensive, city‑encircling perimeter. Modern scholarship estimates its length at roughly twenty‑one miles, far short of the popularly inflated “near fifty miles” (Michels 1995). The wall’s purpose was pragmatic: to protect a densely populated, agriculturally vital hinterland from sudden raids by Germanic tribes who could cross the Tiber valley in a matter of days (Heather 2005). The passage’s footnote to Pliny (⁴⁰) underscores the antiquity of such fortifications, linking Aurelian’s project to a long‑standing Roman tradition of defensive engineering.

### 3. Religious Ritual as Military Supplement

The resort to the Sibylline books and the elaborate processions described—white‑robed priests, choruses of youths and virgins, lustrations—reflects a genuine, if contested, aspect of late‑Roman religiosity. Scholars such as Augustine (c. 400) argue that the empire increasingly turned to “magical” rites as a psychological weapon against barbarian incursions (Augustine, *De Civitate Dei* IV.12). The passage’s acknowledgment that “the powerful influence disabled the barbarians from passing the mystic ground” (line 23) aligns with this view, suggesting that the Romans believed in a spiritual deterrent to enemy morale.

### 4. The Role of Women and Usurpers

The mention of “a female for a long time controlled the fierce legions of Gaul” (line 46) alludes to *Victoria* (also known as *Vulgaris* or *Vulsia*), who, according to Zosimus, ruled after Victorinus’ assassination (Zosimus II.23). Her ability to place “Marius and Tetricus on the throne” (line 48) illustrates the fluidity of imperial legitimacy: power could be derived not solely from military might but from patronage networks and charismatic leadership. The passage implicitly critiques this instability, noting that “the power ended only with her life; but her life was perhaps shortened by the ingratitude of Tetricus” (line 49), a pointed observation about the lack of dynastic cohesion.

### 5. The “Decline of Monarchy” Narrative

The repeated refrain that the “defence of the capital betrayed the decline of monarchy” (line 44) taps into a broader historiographical debate. Historians such as Peter Brown (1975) have argued that the shift from republican ideals to monarchical rule—evident in the deification of emperors and the concentration of power—signaled a fundamental transformation in Roman political culture. The author subtly aligns himself with this view, using the construction of fortifications and reliance on superstition as external manifestations of that internal decay.

---

## III. MAIN ARGUMENT / THESIS

**Thesis.** *The passage contends that, as the late‑Roman state confronted increasingly sophisticated barbarian threats, it turned to two complementary strategies—religious superstition and monumental fortification—both of which reveal a profound erosion of traditional Roman confidence in civic virtue, military might, and monarchical legitimacy.*

In supporting this thesis, the author demonstrates two interlocking points:

1. **Superstition as a Pragmatic War‑Measure.** The invocation of the Sibylline books and the description of elaborate rites suggest that the Romans believed in a supernatural aid that could “disable the barbarians” (line 23). Though the rites are labeled “puerile,” they are framed as “subservient to the success of the war,” indicating a willingness to employ ritual as a psychological weapon when conventional forces were insufficient.

2. **Fortification as a Symbol of Defensive Necessity and Moral Decline.** The construction of the Aurelian Wall—celebrated in popular estimation as near fifty miles yet measured at twenty‑one—signifies both a practical response to security concerns and a lamented departure from the “ideal ramparts” of earlier republican confidence (line 44). The author’s moral framing—“the defence of the capital betrayed the decline of monarchy”—links this architectural endeavor to a broader ethical deterioration.

Together, these elements form a narrative of *compensatory* adaptation: as Rome’s political structures faltered, it turned to supernatural belief and massive, costly defenses, each serving as a surrogate for lost martial prestige. The passage’s balanced use of scholarly citation and emotive language underscores that this shift was not merely a matter of circumstance but a symptom of deepening systemic weakness.

---

## IV. CONCLUSION

The excerpt exemplifies the late‑Roman historian’s blend of antiquarian scholarship and moralizing commentary. By weaving together citations to Pliny, the *Historia Augusta*, and contemporary archaeological measurements, the author constructs an ethos of authority that legitimizes his reading of events. The rhetorical deployment of fear, antithesis, and measured hyperbole heightens the sense of decline, while the footnote apparatus creates a layered, self‑reflexive discourse that invites the reader to question both the historicity of the events and the motives that shaped Roman policy.

Ultimately, the passage argues that the Roman reliance on superstition and the erection of grand fortifications were not isolated tactical responses but emblematic of an empire in which traditional civic virtue had been supplanted by pragmatic, often desperate, measures. In this view, the “decline of monarchy” is not merely a political abstraction but a tangible shift in Roman self‑conception—one that the author, through careful rhetorical orchestration, invites his audience to recognize and mourn.

The emperor presented Zenobia with an elegant villa at Tibur, or       Tivoli, about twenty miles from the capital; the Syrian queen       insensibly sunk into a Roman matron, her daughters married into       noble families, and her race was not yet extinct in the fifth       century. 82 Tetricus and his son were reinstated in their rank       and fortunes. They erected on the Cælian hill a magnificent       palace, and as soon as it was finished, invited Aurelian to       supper. On his entrance, he was agreeably surprised with a       picture which represented their singular history. They were       delineated offering to the emperor a civic crown and the sceptre       of Gaul, and again receiving at his hands the ornaments of the       senatorial dignity. The father was afterwards invested with the       government of Lucania, 83 and Aurelian, who soon admitted the       abdicated monarch to his friendship and conversation, familiarly       asked him, Whether it were not more desirable to administer a       province of Italy, than to reign beyond the Alps. The son long       continued a respectable member of the senate; nor was there any       one of the Roman nobility more esteemed by Aurelian, as well as       by his successors. 84

So long and so various was the pomp of Aurelian’s triumph, that       although it opened with the dawn of day, the slow majesty of the       procession ascended not the Capitol before the ninth hour; and it       was already dark when the emperor returned to the palace. The       festival was protracted by theatrical representations, the games       of the circus, the hunting of wild beasts, combats of gladiators,       and naval engagements. Liberal donatives were distributed to the       army and people, and several institutions, agreeable or       beneficial to the city, contributed to perpetuate the glory of       Aurelian. A considerable portion of his oriental spoils was       consecrated to the gods of Rome; the Capitol, and every other       temple, glittered with the offerings of his ostentatious piety;       and the temple of the Sun alone received above fifteen thousand       pounds of gold. 85 This last was a magnificent structure, erected       by the emperor on the side of the Quirinal hill, and dedicated,       soon after the triumph, to that deity whom Aurelian adored as the       parent of his life and fortunes. His mother had been an inferior       priestess in a chapel of the Sun; a peculiar devotion to the god       of Light was a sentiment which the fortunate peasant imbibed in       his infancy; and every step of his elevation, every victory of       his reign, fortified superstition by gratitude. 86

The arms of Aurelian had vanquished the foreign and domestic foes       of the republic. We are assured, that, by his salutary rigor,       crimes and factions, mischievous arts and pernicious connivance,       the luxurious growth of a feeble and oppressive government, were       eradicated throughout the Roman world. 87 But if we attentively       reflect how much swifter is the progress of corruption than its       cure, and if we remember that the years abandoned to public       disorders exceeded the months allotted to the martial reign of       Aurelian, we must confess that a few short intervals of peace       were insufficient for the arduous work of reformation. Even his       attempt to restore the integrity of the coin was opposed by a       formidable insurrection. The emperor’s vexation breaks out in one       of his private letters. “Surely,” says he, “the gods have decreed       that my life should be a perpetual warfare. A sedition within the       walls has just now given birth to a very serious civil war. The       workmen of the mint, at the instigation of Felicissimus, a slave       to whom I had intrusted an employment in the finances, have risen       in rebellion. They are at length suppressed; but seven thousand       of my soldiers have been slain in the contest, of those troops       whose ordinary station is in Dacia, and the camps along the       Danube.” 88 Other writers, who confirm the same fact, add       likewise, that it happened soon after Aurelian’s triumph; that       the decisive engagement was fought on the Cælian hill; that the       workmen of the mint had adulterated the coin; and that the       emperor restored the public credit, by delivering out good money       in exchange for the bad, which the people was commanded to bring       into the treasury. 89

We might content ourselves with relating this extraordinary       transaction, but we cannot dissemble how much in its present form       it appears to us inconsistent and incredible. The debasement of       the coin is indeed well suited to the administration of       Gallienus; nor is it unlikely that the instruments of the       corruption might dread the inflexible justice of Aurelian. But       the guilt, as well as the profit, must have been confined to a       very few; nor is it easy to conceive by what arts they could arm       a people whom they had injured, against a monarch whom they had       betrayed. We might naturally expect that such miscreants should       have shared the public detestation with the informers and the       other ministers of oppression; and that the reformation of the       coin should have been an action equally popular with the       destruction of those obsolete accounts, which by the emperor’s       order were burnt in the forum of Trajan. 90 In an age when the       principles of commerce were so imperfectly understood, the most       desirable end might perhaps be effected by harsh and injudicious       means; but a temporary grievance of such a nature can scarcely       excite and support a serious civil war. The repetition of       intolerable taxes, imposed either on the land or on the       necessaries of life, may at last provoke those who will not, or       who cannot, relinquish their country. But the case is far       otherwise in every operation which, by whatsoever expedients,       restores the just value of money. The transient evil is soon       obliterated by the permanent benefit, the loss is divided among       multitudes; and if a few wealthy individuals experience a       sensible diminution of treasure, with their riches, they at the       same time lose the degree of weight and importance which they       derived from the possession of them. However Aurelian might       choose to disguise the real cause of the insurrection, his       reformation of the coin could furnish only a faint pretence to a       party already powerful and discontented. Rome, though deprived of       freedom, was distracted by faction. The people, towards whom the       emperor, himself a plebeian, always expressed a peculiar       fondness, lived in perpetual dissension with the senate, the       equestrian order, and the Prætorian guards. 91 Nothing less than       the firm though secret conspiracy of those orders, of the       authority of the first, the wealth of the second, and the arms of       the third, could have displayed a strength capable of contending       in battle with the veteran legions of the Danube, which, under       the conduct of a martial sovereign, had achieved the conquest of       the West and of the East.

Whatever was the cause or the object of this rebellion, imputed       with so little probability to the workmen of the mint, Aurelian       used his victory with unrelenting rigor. 92 He was naturally of a       severe disposition. A peasant and a soldier, his nerves yielded       not easily to the impressions of sympathy, and he could sustain       without emotion the sight of tortures and death. Trained from his       earliest youth in the exercise of arms, he set too small a value       on the life of a citizen, chastised by military execution the       slightest offences, and transferred the stern discipline of the       camp into the civil administration of the laws. His love of       justice often became a blind and furious passion; and whenever he       deemed his own or the public safety endangered, he disregarded       the rules of evidence, and the proportion of punishments. The       unprovoked rebellion with which the Romans rewarded his services,       exasperated his haughty spirit. The noblest families of the       capital were involved in the guilt or suspicion of this dark       conspiracy. A nasty spirit of revenge urged the bloody       prosecution, and it proved fatal to one of the nephews of the       emperor. 2. **The futility of such a fortification.**

The oldest of the citizens, recollecting the spectacles       of former days, the triumphal pomp of Probus or Aurelian, and the       secular games of the emperor Philip, acknowledged that they were       all surpassed by the superior magnificence of Carinus. 84

The spectacles of Carinus may therefore be best illustrated by       the observation of some particulars, which history has       condescended to relate concerning those of his predecessors. The passage is a tightly‑woven encomium of Diocletian and a vilification of his rivals.

Aper, the prefect who tried to secure Numerian’s election, is cast as a murderer whose “crime” is proved on the spot. The passage repeatedly labels them “cruel”, “arrogant”, “ungrateful”, and “disliked by the people and the Senate”. |
| **Diocletian is the rightful, divinely‑sanctioned restorer of order** | Diocletian’s rise is framed as a necessary corrective: he is urged to “revenging and succeeding” his beloved emperor, he invokes the Sun as a witness of his innocence, and the legions acclaim him as the “justice and authority” of the empire. In short, the author argues that the chaotic aftermath of Carus’s death can only be resolved by eliminating corrupt usurpers and placing a man of proven moral character and divine favor—Diocletian—on the throne. The passage therefore serves as imperial propaganda: it supplies a moral justification for Diocletian’s accession and for the purge of his opponents.

**2. Rhetorical style**

The passage is a textbook example of the panegyrical, moralising historiography that characterises much of late‑antique Roman historiography (especially the *Historia Augusta*). Its style can be broken down into several recognisable devices:

| Rhetorical device | Example in the text | Effect |
|-------------------|----------------------|--------|
| **Hyperbole & Vivid Imagery** | “glittering pageantry”, “the divine graces of his person”, “the solitude and darkness of a tent or litter”. | Heightens the contrast between the emperor’s public adulation and the grim reality of war‑fatigued troops; creates a dramatic moral tableau. |
| **Antithesis & Parallelism** | “the flattery of his courtiers, and the songs of the poets” (parallel); “the empire … was engaged in favour of his rival, and even the senate was inclined to prefer a usurper to a tyrant” (antithesis of “favour” vs. “usurper”). | Emphasises the duality of public perception—popular acclaim versus hidden corruption. |
| **Moral Condemnation & Encomium** | Repeated epithets: “unworthy”, “tyrant”, “cruel arrogance” for Carinus; “affable manners”, “gentle virtues”, “elegant accomplishments” for Numerian; “just and righteous ruler” for Diocletian. | Aligns the reader emotionally on one side (the usurpers) and the other (the rightful emperor). |
| **Divine Symbolism** | “raising his eyes towards the Sun, made a solemn profession of his own innocence, in the presence of that all‑seeing Deity”. | Invokes the *sol invictus* cult and the idea that Diocletian’s authority is sanctioned by the gods, a common rhetorical move in late‑imperial legitimation. |
| **Causal‑temporal linking** | “The gradual decline of his health might have induced them to believe that his death was natural; but the concealment was interpreted as an evidence of guilt…”; “the future fortunes of the candidate depended on the chance or conduct of the present hour.” | Shows a logical chain from Numerian’s illness → suspicion → Aper’s downfall → Diocletian’s accession, presenting events as inevitable and sanctioned. |
| **Repetition & Anaphora** | “the emperor Carinus” appears three times at the start of successive clauses; “the empire” and “the people” recur throughout. | Reinforces the central figure and creates a rhythmic, almost liturgical cadence. |
| **Narrative Authority** | The passage presents itself as a “proper” account (“Before we enter upon the memorable reign of that prince, it will be proper to punish…”) and uses the voice of the historian as a moral judge. | Positions the author as a trustworthy chronicler whose job is to separate virtue from vice. |

The overall tone is that of *encomium* (praise) for Diocletian blended with *invidia* (disgust) for his opponents. The rhetorical flourishes are not neutral reportage; they are deliberately designed to mould the reader’s perception of who belongs on the throne and why.

| **The purge of potential rivals (Aper)** | The swift execution of Aper—“the murderer of Numerian”—is framed as a necessary judicial act that secures Diocletian’s rule. | This mirrors real events: Aper, a senior prefect, was indeed executed in 284 after being blamed for Numerian’s death. | **The civil war at Margus (284)** | The narrative mentions Carinus’s defeat after “infidelity of his officers” and a “tribune… extinguished civil discord in the blood of the adulterer.” | The actual battle of Margus ended Diocletian’s rival in the east; the passage dramatizes it to stress the volatility of the period and the eventual triumph of the “rightful” emperor. |

**Why the passage matters to us today**

- **Propaganda vs. History:** The text shows how early imperial biographies were shaped as much by the needs of the regime (legitimising Diocletian’s accession, discrediting rivals) as by “objective” reporting.  
- **Military‑Political Dynamics:** It highlights the growing dependence of Roman emperors on the army’s acclamation, a trend that would culmininate in the *military* crises of the 4th c.  
- **The Tetrarchic Ideology:** By presenting Diocletian as the natural successor who restores order, the passage anticipates the tetrarchy’s core idea: divide rule to prevent usurpation, but only under a single, divinely‑endorsed “senior” emperor.

The passage argues that Diocletian’s accession was not merely a matter of chance but a divinely‑ordained solution to the moral and political chaos left by Carinus and Numerian. ### 1. Main Argument

The passage argues that **Carausius’s usurpation in Britain, although initially successful and marked by impressive naval power and a brief alliance with the Franks, was ultimately crushed by the Roman state through a combination of military force, strategic fortifications, and the administrative reforms introduced by Diocletian**.

1. **The Threat Posed by Carausius** – Britain’s wealth and strategic position make its loss a serious blow; Carausius exploits this by building a fleet, seizing Boulogne, and aligning himself with the Franks, thereby threatening Roman control of the Channel and the continent.

2. **Roman Counter‑measures** – Diocletian’s policy of fortifying the frontiers, encouraging internal barbarian conflict, and dividing imperial authority restores Roman military superiority. Constantius leads a decisive naval campaign under the praetorian prefect Asclepiodatus, defeats Allectus (the usurper’s lieutenant), and forces the Britons to submit, restoring Britain to the empire after ten years of separation.

3. **Broader Imperial Implications** – The episode illustrates the effectiveness of Diocletian’s reforms: a strong, centrally‑directed navy, fortified riverine frontiers, and a political strategy that turns potential enemies against one another. The successful suppression of Carausius is presented as proof that the late‑Roman state could still project power and maintain stability in the face of both internal usurpations and external barbarian pressures.

Thus the central claim is that **the Roman Empire’s institutional and military adaptability under Diocletian’s tetrarchy allowed it to overcome the usurper’s maritime ambitions and re‑integrate Britain firmly within the imperial system**.

The avenues of the palace were       strictly guarded by the various schools, as they began to be       called, of domestic officers. As he wished       to secure the obedience of Maximian, he exacted from him either a       general assurance that he would submit his actions to the       authority of his benefactor, or a particular promise that he       would descend from the throne, whenever he should receive the       advice and the example. This engagement, though it was confirmed       by the solemnity of an oath before the altar of the Capitoline       Jupiter, 110 would have proved a feeble restraint on the fierce       temper of Maximian, whose passion was the love of power, and who       neither desired present tranquility nor future reputation. But he       yielded, however reluctantly, to the ascendant which his wiser       colleague had acquired over him, and retired, immediately after       his abdication, to a villa in Lucania, where it was almost       impossible that such an impatient spirit could find any lasting       tranquility.

Diocletian, who, from a servile origin, had raised himself to the       throne, passed the nine last years of his life in a private       condition. Reason had dictated, and content seems to have       accompanied, his retreat, in which he enjoyed, for a long time,       the respect of those princes to whom he had resigned the       possession of the world. 111 It is seldom that minds long       exercised in business have formed any habits of conversing with       themselves, and in the loss of power they principally regret the       want of occupation. The amusements of letters and of devotion,       which afford so many resources in solitude, were incapable of       fixing the attention of Diocletian; but he had preserved, or at       least he soon recovered, a taste for the most innocent as well as       natural pleasures, and his leisure hours were sufficiently       employed in building, planting, and gardening. His answer to       Maximian is deservedly celebrated. He was solicited by that       restless old man to reassume the reins of government, and the       Imperial purple. He rejected the temptation with a smile of pity,       calmly observing, that if he could show Maximian the cabbages       which he had planted with his own hands at Salona, he should no       longer be urged to relinquish the enjoyment of happiness for the       pursuit of power. 112 In his conversations with his friends, he       frequently acknowledged, that of all arts, the most difficult was       the art of reigning; and he expressed himself on that favorite       topic with a degree of warmth which could be the result only of       experience. “How often,” was he accustomed to say, “is it the       interest of four or five ministers to combine together to deceive       their sovereign! He       confers the most important offices upon vice and weakness, and       disgraces the most virtuous and deserving among his subjects. Though Constantine, from a very obvious prejudice, affects to       mention the palace of Diocletian with contempt, 118 yet one of       their successors, who could only see it in a neglected and       mutilated state, celebrates its magnificence in terms of the       highest admiration. 119 It covered an extent of ground consisting       of between nine and ten English acres. The form was quadrangular,       flanked with sixteen towers. Two of the sides were near six       hundred, and the other two near seven hundred feet in length. The       whole was constructed of a beautiful freestone, extracted from       the neighboring quarries of Trau, or Tragutium, and very little       inferior to marble itself. Four streets, intersecting each other       at right angles, divided the several parts of this great edifice,       and the approach to the principal apartment was from a very       stately entrance, which is still denominated the Golden Gate. The       approach was terminated by a _peristylium_ of granite columns, on       one side of which we discover the square temple of Æsculapius, on       the other the octagon temple of Jupiter. The latter of those       deities Diocletian revered as the patron of his fortunes, the       former as the protector of his health. By comparing the present       remains with the precepts of Vitruvius, the several parts of the       building, the baths, bedchamber, the _atrium_, the _basilica_,       and the Cyzicene, Corinthian, and Egyptian halls have been       described with some degree of precision, or at least of       probability. Their forms were various, their proportions just;       but they all were attended with two imperfections, very repugnant       to our modern notions of taste and conveniency. These stately       rooms had neither windows nor chimneys. They were lighted from       the top, (for the building seems to have consisted of no more       than one story,) and they received their heat by the help of       pipes that were conveyed along the walls. The range of principal       apartments was protected towards the south-west by a portico five       hundred and seventeen feet long, which must have formed a very       noble and delightful walk, when the beauties of painting and       sculpture were added to those of the prospect.

Had this magnificent edifice remained in a solitary country, it       would have been exposed to the ravages of time; but it might,       perhaps, have escaped the rapacious industry of man. The village       of Aspalathus, 120 and, long afterwards, the provincial town of       Spalatro, have grown out of its ruins. The Golden Gate now opens       into the market-place. St. John the Baptist has usurped the       honors of Æsculapius; and the temple of Jupiter, under the       protection of the Virgin, is converted into the cathedral church.

For this account of Diocletian’s palace we are principally       indebted to an ingenious artist of our own time and country, whom       a very liberal curiosity carried into the heart of Dalmatia. 121       But there is room to suspect that the elegance of his designs and       engraving has somewhat flattered the objects which it was their       purpose to represent. We are informed by a more recent and very       judicious traveller, that the awful ruins of Spalatro are not       less expressive of the decline of the art than of the greatness       of the Roman empire in the time of Diocletian. 122 If such was       indeed the state of architecture, we must naturally believe that       painting and sculpture had experienced a still more sensible       decay. The practice of architecture is directed by a few general       and even mechanical rules. He has first bridged the abyss between ancient and       modern times, and connected together the two great worlds of       history. Natural unity confined their narrative almost to       chronological order, the episodes were of rare occurrence and       extremely brief. To the Roman historians the course was equally       clear and defined. Rome was their centre of unity; and the       uniformity with which the circle of the Roman dominion spread       around, the regularity with which their civil polity expanded,       forced, as it were, upon the Roman historian that plan which       Polybius announces as the subject of his history, the means and       the manner by which the whole world became subject to the Roman       sway. We feel that the unity and harmony of narrative, which shall       comprehend this period of social disorganization, must be       ascribed entirely to the skill and luminous disposition of the       historian. II. The insolence of the armies inspired Augustus with fears of a       still more alarming nature. The despair of the citizens could       only attempt, what the power of the soldiers was, at any time,       able to execute. 3. **The mythic façade is hollow and self‑defeating.**  By styling himself “Roman Hercules” and surrounding his throne with the attributes of the god, Commodus attempts to win popular approval, but the author shows that the façade cannot mask the emperor’s “extinct … sentiments of virtue and humanity.” The very public displays of cruelty (slaying lions, ostriches, elephants) reinforce the perception that he is a ferocious beast rather than a beneficent ruler. Historically, the Praetorian Guard, instituted by Augustus to protect the emperor and enforce imperial authority, had become a tool of political intrigue. The author’s observation that “the power of the sword is more sensibly felt in an extensive monarchy” reflects contemporary Roman thought about the balance between military might and civilian governance—a concern amplified by the recent memory of civil wars and the precariousness of imperial legitimacy.

Finally, the moral framing—declaring that even a guilty senator should not be “stained by the blood”—appeals to the Roman ideal of *clementia* (clemency), reinforcing the notion that true authority derives from moral legitimacy rather than coercive force.

Thus, the text uses moral contrast, cataloguing, and appeals to Roman virtues to critique the erosion of republican values under imperial autocracy, reflecting the tumultuous political climate in which the Praetorian Guard’s rise and fall became decisive factors in the empire’s instability.

### 1.  Main argument

The passage sets out a clear, though highly partisan, explanation of why the brief reign of Emperor Julian was doomed. In the author’s view the revolt of these commanders was **inevitable once the emperor lost the confidence of the people and the legions**, and it doomed not only Julian but also the whole “public peace”.  

The argument proceeds in three steps:

1. **The emperor’s isolation** – Julian is portrayed as standing “without a friend, and even without an adherent”; the guards are ashamed of him, the citizens view his accession with horror, and the populace vents its fury in the streets.  
2. **The diffusion of discontent** – The emperor’s unpopularity spreads from the capital to the frontiers, where the legions of Britain, Syria and Illyricum “lamented the death of Pertinax” and refused the Praetorian bargain.  
3. **The generals’ revolt** – Albinus, Niger and Severus, each commanding three legions, are described as equally powerful yet equally self‑interested; their simultaneous uprisings bring about Julian’s downfall and, at the same time, tear the empire apart.

Thus the passage argues that **imperial legitimacy in the Roman world rested on the consent of the governed and the loyalty of the army**; once those were lost, the emperor could be displaced by military usurpers, and the empire would slip into civil war.

2. **The role of the legions** – In the early‑imperial period the loyalty of the provincial legions could make or break an emperor.  The passage stresses that the legions of Britain, Syria and Illyricum “lamented” Pertinax’s death, showing how the death of a brief emperor could instantly mobilise entire armies against his successor.  This reflects the well‑documented fact that military commanders often acted as power‑brokers, not merely as administrators.

3. **Praetorian Guard’s political power** – The “public auction” of the empire is a direct allusion to the real episode of 69 AD when the Guard attempted to sell the throne to the highest bidder (the future Emperor Galba, according to some sources). 6. **The “Year of the Four Emperors” as a paradigm of imperial weakness** – The author implicitly uses the events of 69 AD as a cautionary paradigm: when the emperor loses popular support, the army fragments, and civil war follows.  This theme resonated in the 3rd‑century crisis (the “Crisis of the Third Century”), when rapid succession, usurpations, and the auction of the throne became all too familiar.

### 4.  Synthesis

The passage presents a **deterministic view of imperial power**: legitimacy is not an inherent right of the emperor but a function of popular assent and military loyalty.  By dramatising Julian’s isolation, the spread of discontent to the frontiers, and the opportunistic revolt of three equally powerful generals, the author argues that **the emperor’s downfall was inevitable once he lost the confidence of the people and the legions**. The passage tells us that, after the fall of the Roman Republic, the emperor was not a hereditary monarch ruling by birthright but a *popular candidate* whose legitimacy depended on the support of the legions. In other words, the “people” (more precisely, the soldiers) could make any victorious general emperor, and once a man had the army behind him he could be proclaimed “the candidate of the people.” However, this “popular” support was purely transactional:

* **No principle or ideology** – The troops fought for personal loyalty, reward (donatives and promises), fear of defeat, or a chance to plunder, not for any abstract notion of liberty, religion, or constitutional right.
* **No broad popular sovereignty** – The provinces had no real voice; they submitted to whichever emperor could offer security and clemency.
* **The civil wars were therefore** a contest of personal ambition and the army’s self‑interest, not a clash of principled factions as in modern European wars.

Thus, the Roman Empire functioned as a “popular candidate for empire” only in the narrow sense that the emperor’s rule was sustained by the popular (military) will, but that will was not an expression of democratic principle; it was a pragmatic, self‑interested loyalty to a strong commander.

2. **The army’s motives** – When Severus faced usurpers (Niger, Albinus), his troops were motivated by:
   * *Affection* for a benefactor,
   * *Fear* of reprisals,
   * *Interest* in the donatives and promises that accompanied a change of regime.

3. **Absence of fortified resistance** – The empire’s geography (few fortified cities, vast distances) meant that a defeated usurper could not rely on a popular uprising to rally a new base; the only viable response was to desert the losing cause and submit to the victorious commander.

4. **Contrast with modern civil wars** – The passage explicitly notes that European civil wars were driven by “religion, freedom, or loyalty,” with leaders drawing on hereditary property and noble influence. **1. Purpose of the source**  
The passage is employed by Hume (1748) as a historical illustration in his *Essay on the Populosity of Ancient Nations*. His broader thesis concerns the demographic decline of the ancient world, which he attributes in part to the endemic violence of imperial politics. By presenting the murder of Geta and the subsequent wave of repression under Caracalla, Hume seeks to demonstrate that the Roman state was a “machine of cruelty” whose internal conflicts contributed to a chronic loss of life and, consequently, to the stagnation of population (Hume, Essay II.4). The source therefore functions as evidential support for a structural argument about the relationship between political brutality and demographic decline.

**2. Rhetorical structure of the passage**  
Hume organizes the text in a progressive, cause‑and‑effect pattern:  

1. **Establishing the context** – He cites Herodian (l. iv. p. 139) and other antiquarians to set the spatial and political background of imperial gardens and the proximity of the palace to the rest of Rome.  
2. **Narrating the treaty and its breakdown** – The proposed division of the empire between Caracalla and Geta is described in terms of “mutual benefit” and “conditions of the treaty,” foregrounding the political motive for separation.  
3. **The murder of Geta** – A vivid, emotionally charged scene (centurions’ ambush, Julia’s wound, Caracalla’s flight to the Praetorian camp) serves as the climax of the narrative.  
4. **Immediate political fallout** – Caracalla’s proclamation of his “cause” and the distribution of a massive donative illustrate how the murder is transformed into a legitimising act for the emperor.  
5. **Broadening to a pattern of oppression** – The passage then lists further executions (Helvius Pertinax, Thrasea Priscus) and the scale of the proscriptions, thereby moving from a single act to a systemic pattern.  

The rhetorical devices employed include:  
* **Enumeration** (e.g., “gardens of Sallust, Lucullus, Agrippa…”) to overwhelm the reader with evidence of imperial control.  
* **Emotive language** (tears, blood, guilt) to evoke sympathy for the victims and moral condemnation of the perpetrators.  
* **Appeal to authority** (references to Herodian, Victor, Nardini) to lend the narrative an air of scholarly credibility.  
* **Causal linking** (the murder “required the most forcible violence” to be torn asunder; “the consciousness of his crime” leads to further repression) to construct a deterministic view of imperial brutality.  

**3. Author’s view of Caracalla’s motives and the precise nature of his crime**  
Hume interprets Caracalla’s actions as driven by *ambition* and *self‑preservation*. The emperor “listened to his mother’s entreaties” and “consented to meet his brother in her apartment” on the pretext of reconciliation, yet the ambush reveals a pre‑meditated, opportunistic killing (Hume, Essay II.4). The crime is described as a *treacherous assassination*: centurions concealed themselves, struck Geta while he conversed with his mother, and Caracalla fled to the Praetorian camp, then used the murder to consolidate power by presenting himself as the defender of the empire. The passage also highlights the *political motive* of preventing a permanent division of the empire, suggesting that Caracalla’s act was not a personal vendetta but a calculated step to secure sole rulership (Hume, Essay II.4).

**4. Evidence supporting the claim that Geta’s murder was part of a larger pattern of violence and oppression**  
Hume builds his argument on a series of corroborating incidents:  

* **Proscriptions and mass killings** – “above twenty thousand persons of both sexes suffered death” because of alleged connections to Geta, illustrating a systematic purge of perceived political enemies (Hume, Essay II.4).  
* **Targeted executions of prominent senators** – Helvius Pertinax, a son of a former emperor, is killed by a “witticism,” and Thrasea Priscus is executed for his republican sympathies, demonstrating that dissent was punished regardless of rank (Hume, Essay II.4).  
* **Political manipulation after the murder** – Caracalla’s distribution of a “lavish donative” and the subsequent “obsequious” Senate’s ratification of his rule show how violence was transformed into legitimising authority.  
* **Continuity with earlier imperial excesses** – The mention of “imperial gardens” and the confiscation of senatorial estates under preceding emperors (Sallust, Lucullus, Domitian) places Geta’s murder within a tradition of using land and wealth as tools of control, suggesting a structural rather than isolated phenomenon.  

Together, these examples create a cumulative picture of imperial brutality: the assassination of a brother, the ensuing proscriptions, and the broader climate of fear and repression constitute a pattern of violence that Hume uses to support his demographic thesis.

Is it possible to relate without an indignant       smile, that, on the father’s decease, the property of a nation,       like that of a drove of oxen, descends to his infant son, as yet       unknown to mankind and to himself; and that the bravest warriors       and the wisest statesmen, relinquishing their natural right to       empire, approach the royal cradle with bended knees and       protestations of inviolable fidelity? Satire and declamation may       paint these obvious topics in the most dazzling colors, but our       more serious thoughts will respect a useful prejudice, that       establishes a rule of succession, independent of the passions of       mankind; and we shall cheerfully acquiesce in any expedient which       deprives the multitude of the dangerous, and indeed the ideal,       power of giving themselves a master.

Experience overturns these airy fabrics,       and teaches us, that in a large society, the election of a       monarch can never devolve to the wisest, or to the most numerous       part of the people. The acknowledged       right extinguishes the hopes of faction, and the conscious       security disarms the cruelty of the monarch. To the firm       establishment of this idea we owe the peaceful succession and       mild administration of European monarchies. After the murder of Alexander Severus, and the elevation of       Maximin, no emperor could think himself safe upon the throne, and       every barbarian peasant of the frontier might aspire to that       august, but dangerous station.

About thirty‑two years before a famous battle, Emperor Severus was on his way back from the East. He stopped in Thrace to celebrate the birthday of his younger son, Geta, with a big military games festival. The whole country turned out to watch their ruler, and a hulking young Thracian who spoke only a rough dialect begged to be let him try his hand at wrestling.  

The emperor’s men—big, stout soldiers—were paired against him. He knocked out sixteen of them in turn. For his trouble he got a few trinkets and a place in the imperial guard. The next day everyone cheered him on like a local hero, dancing the Thracian way.  

Seeing that the emperor was paying attention, the youth galloped to his horse, ran alongside the emperor on foot, and never seemed out of breath. “Thracian,” Severus exclaimed, “do you want to keep wrestling after that run?”  

“Sure thing, sir,” the youth panted, and almost in one breath he tossed seven of the strongest soldiers to the ground. A gold collar—his prize—was slapped on him, and he was promoted to the emperor’s horse guards.

**Maximinus Thrace: From Barbarian Rookie to Imperial Pretender**

Maximinus was born in the empire but came from mixed barbarian parents—his father a Goth, his mother an Alani. He was brave, quick, and had a fierce streak, but he also learned the ways of Rome. Under Severus and his son, he rose to centurion, earning the respect of both princes. He refused to serve under the assassin Caracalla and sneered at the effeminate Emperor Elagabalus.  

When Alexander Severus took the throne, Maximinus was put in charge of the fourth legion. He turned it into the best‑trained unit in the whole army, and the soldiers started calling him Ajax and Hercules. He kept climbing the ladder until he was the top military commander.

---

**A Rising Ambition Turns Into Rebellion**

The Thracian who had wrestled at Geta’s birthday felt his status wasn’t enough. He saw the emperor’s loss of favor with the troops and decided to stir up discontent. He wasn’t a deep thinker, but he knew a thing or two about how to use the soldiers’ anger.

The army, weary of the soft rule of the Syrian emperor—who seemed more a scared slave than a true leader—began demanding a real soldier as their leader. A massive force was gathered on the Rhine under the emperor himself, fresh from his Persian campaign. Maximinus was tasked with training the new recruits.

One day, as he entered the training field, the soldiers—either in a sudden flash or as part of a plot—shouted “Long live the emperor!” Maximinus tried to refuse, but the roar of the crowd drowned him out. He was quickly declared emperor, and together with his supporters, they murdered Alexander Severus.

---

**What Really Happened to Maximinus?**

Two main stories survive about his death. One says he died without knowing the treachery of Maximinus. After a simple meal, he went to sleep, and around the seventh hour his own guard broke into his tent and killed him with many wounds.

A more likely version tells that Maximinus was actually crowned emperor at a distance from the main camp. He trusted in secret wishes rather than public proclamations. Alexander managed to get a flicker of loyalty from the troops, but as soon as Maximinus showed up, promising to champion the soldiers, the legionnaires shouted him as emperor. Alexander’s son, Mamæa’s son, tried to hide, but was soon surrounded by a tribune and centurions sent to finish the job. He begged and pleaded, but was ultimately killed, and his mother, Mamæa, died with him. The emperor’s closest friends were sacrificed, others were cruelly executed, and many were stripped of rank and banished.

---

**Why Did Maximinus Go So Far?**

Unlike the earlier tyrants—Caligula, Nero, Commodus, Caracalla—who were young, spoiled emperors corrupted by luxury and flattery, Maximinus’s cruelty came from fear. He knew he was a barbarian outsider, rough‑looking and uneducated, while Alexander was a polished, beloved ruler. Maximinus remembered being turned away by Roman nobles when he was poor, and how a few friends had helped him rise. He felt that anyone who knew his low birth could be his downfall. So he ruthlessly eliminated those who had ever helped him, sending a bloody message that even his benefactors were guilty of his “low‑born” origins.

Severus’s nephew Maximinus, a Thracian soldier with mixed barbarian roots, rose through the ranks under the emperor’s sons, became a beloved commander, and then, using the discontent of a tired army, declared himself emperor and killed Alexander Severus. He ruled with harsh, often brutal, methods because he feared that his own humble background made him vulnerable to the Roman elite. His reign ended in a palace‑style coup, and he met a violent end surrounded by betrayals and bloodshed.

### 1. Overview  

Text 59 is a compact, highly rhetorical vignette that presents the joint reign of the “new emperors” Maximus and Balbinus as the embodiment of Roman virtue and legitimacy. It praises their personal qualities, political experience, and public service, then dramatizes the popular unrest that threatens their rule. The narrative subsequently turns to the antagonist, Emperor Maximin Thrax, describing him as a savage usurper whose cruelty and ambition endanger the Republic. The passage is peppered with footnote references (Herodian, Censorinus, Eckhel, etc.) that reveal the author’s reliance on earlier historiographical sources and his awareness of chronological disputes.

The text serves three inter‑related purposes:

1. **Defence of Maximus and Balbinus** – to argue that they deserve the people’s support and that a third emperor from the Gordian family is a just concession.  
2. **Condemnation of Maximin** – to cast him as a tyrant whose barbarism justifies opposition.  
3. **Historical Legitimisation** – to ground the argument in ostensible authority (senatorial decree, religious titles, and ancient historiography) while subtly shaping the reader’s moral judgment.

### 2. Main Argument  

The author’s central claim can be summarised as follows:

> *Maximus and Balbinus, as senior, experienced, and virtuous consuls, were the rightful co‑rulers of Rome; the popular demand for a third emperor from the Gordian line is both a moral imperative and a political necessity, whereas Maximin, a merciless war‑lord, is an illegitimate usurper whose savage character must be opposed.*

The argument is built on a **contrastive moral schema**:

| Element | Maximus & Balbinus | Maximin |
|---|---|---|
| **Origin** | Noble birth, affluent fortune, liberal manners | Meanest origin, risen by military might |
| **Virtues** | Oratory, poetry, jurisprudence, austerity, impartial justice | Austerity (in appearance) but ruthless pragmatism; “savage” cruelty |
| **Public Reception** | Popular affection, “the people’s affections engaged” | Hostility, “licentious multitude” hostile to his rigour |

| **Outcome** | Murdered by the people (but portrayed as martyrs) | Assassinated by his own troops near Aquileia |

The author seeks to persuade the reader that the **senatorial decision to add a third emperor from the Gordian family** is not merely a political maneuver but a **moral restitution**: the Gordians had “sacrificed their lives for the republic”, and their descendants deserve a share in power.

* **Vivid sensory detail** – “the multitude, armed with sticks and stones, drove them back into the Capitol” (parallelism of *sticks* and *stones*).

**1. Main argument**  
The author argues that the fall of the tyrant Maximin in 235 CE was a pivotal turning point that ended a period of oppression and restored Roman liberty, and that this event was achieved through a combination of local resistance (Aquileia’s steadfast citizens), internal conspiracies, and the strategic restraint of Maximus and his co‑emperors. The narrative presents Maximin as a brutal, almost monstrous ruler whose cruelty, famine‑driven ruin and mismanagement provoked both the desertion of the populace and the eventual betrayal of his own troops, leading to his death and the renewal of a more humane imperial order.

**2. Main points (summary)**  
- Maximin’s army, marching through Italy, met the deserted and impoverished frontier, where the senate’s policy of famine and siege aimed to weaken him.  
- Aquileia’s citizens, spurred by Crispinus and Menophilus, held out despite the city’s weakened walls; their morale was bolstered by the belief that the god Belenus fought for them.  
- Maximus, at Ravenna, feared that a prolonged siege would allow Maximin’s forces to turn toward Rome; he tried to raise new troops but was uneasy about their reliability.  
- Troops of Maximin suffered disease, famine, and demoralisation, while Aquileians enjoyed plentiful supplies and water.  
- A Praetorian guard plot murdered Maximin, killing his son Anulinus and ministers; the news of their decapitation convinced the besieged troops that the siege was over.  
- After Maximin’s death, Maximus and his co‑emperors (Balbinus and Gordian) entered Rome triumphantly, repealed oppressive taxes, revived discipline, and began restoring a civil constitution.  
- The fall of Maximin sparked universal joy across the empire, with the news reaching Rome in four days and prompting a hopeful expectation of a golden age.

**3. Text analysis (description of the passage)**  
The passage is a carefully staged historical narrative that blends factual reportage with vivid, almost rhetorical, details about geography, weather, and architecture. It moves from a description of Maximin’s advance and the senate’s strategic sabotage, through the siege of Aquileia, to the internal conspiracy that ends Maximin’s reign, and finally to the triumphal return of Maximus and the restoration of Roman order. The author interweaves concrete images (e.g., “large hogsheads” bridge, “streams swelled by melting snow”) with moral judgments (“the tyrant’s unrelenting temper,” “brutal savage lacking humanity”).

**4. Rhetorical devices**  
- **Anaphora:** Repetition of “the walls…had been hastily repaired,” “the troops…exposed to,” “the oppressive taxes…were repealed.”  
- **Parallelism:** “Some troops newly levied…and a body of German auxiliaries.”  
- **Personification:** “the streams…opposed an unexpected obstacle,” “the city’s constancy…supported and directed by Crispinus and Menophilus.”  
- **Allusion:** Reference to Belenus as a personal deity defending the city, and to the “golden age” versus “age of iron.”  
- **Hyperbole:** Descriptions of Maximin’s height (“exceeded eight feet”) and strength, presented as almost mythic.  
- **Contrast:** Sharp juxtaposition between the comfort of Aquileians and the misery of Maximin’s soldiers.  
- **Appeal to authority:** Citing senatorial generals as wise, and the Praetorian guards as the agents of justice.  

**5. Historical events/situations**  
- **Year:** 235 CE (the final years of the Crisis of the Third Century).  
- **Maximinus Thrax:** Roman emperor (235‑238), known for heavy taxation, cruelty, and reliance on Germanic troops.  
- **Aquileia siege:** Part of Maximin’s campaign against the eastern frontier; the city’s resistance is historically attested.  
- **Praetorian Guard conspiracy:** The murder of Maximin by a faction of his own guards, leading to his death on 19 March 238.  
- **Maximus and Balbinus:** Co‑emperors after Maximin’s death; Maximus (r. 238‑241) pursued reforms, while Balbinus (r. 238‑241) was more moderate.  
- **Crisis of the Third Century:** Rapid turnover of emperors, economic collapse, and the rise of military usurpers.  

**6. Evaluation of source reliability/bias**  
The passage appears to be a secondary literary reconstruction, likely derived from histories such as those of Herodian or Eutropius, rather than a contemporary official chronicle. Its vivid language and moral framing suggest an agenda to portray Maximin as a monstrous tyrant whose downfall was both just and necessary for Rome’s salvation. The emphasis on civic virtue (Aquileian constancy) and the depiction of Maximus as a “wise” ruler reflect a bias toward celebrating senatorial and imperial restoration over the chaos of civil war. Nevertheless, the core events—siege of Aquileia, Praetorian murder of Maximin, and the triumphal return of Maximus—are corroborated by multiple ancient sources, lending a degree of factual reliability despite the rhetorical embellishments.
